lines: Who Peter was.
Peter is one of the most famous people who ever lived, but he started out as an ordinary working man.
He was born with the name Simon, son of John (sometimes written Jonah), and he grew up in Bethsaida, a small fishing village on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee in northern Israel.
Later he moved a few miles west to Capernaum, a busier lakeside town, where he had his own house.
Throughout this story we call him Peter, the name Jesus gave him, even though his friends and family would have called him Simon at first.
Peter was a fisherman, and so was his younger brother Andrew.
Fishing on the Sea of Galilee was hard, dangerous work.
The lake is about 13 miles long and 8 miles wide, and violent storms can come up suddenly when wind pours down from the surrounding hills.
Fishermen usually worked at night, throwing heavy nets from wooden boats, then spent the morning washing and mending them.
Peter and Andrew ran their business together with two other brothers, James and John, the sons of Zebedee.
Luke calls them “partners.”
Peter was married.
The Gospels never tell us his wife’s name, but they mention his mother-in-law, who lived with them, and Paul later says that Peter’s wife traveled with him when he was a church leader.
He was not a scholar, a priest, or a rabbi.
Years later, when Peter was arrested and stood before the most powerful religious leaders in Jerusalem, they looked at him and saw an “unschooled, ordinary” man.
He spoke Aramaic with a strong Galilean accent that people in Jerusalem noticed right away.
From everything the Bible records, Peter was bold, emotional, quick to speak and quick to act.
He often said what everyone else was thinking, sometimes brilliantly and sometimes foolishly.
He was also deeply loyal.
That mix of courage and weakness is what makes his story so human.
How Peter met Jesus.
Peter did not meet Jesus by accident.
His brother Andrew had become a follower of John the Baptist, the desert prophet who was preaching that people needed to turn back to God because the promised Messiah was coming.
Many Galileans traveled south to the Jordan River to hear John, and Peter may have gone too.
One day John saw Jesus walking by and said, “Look, the Lamb of God!”
Andrew and another disciple immediately followed Jesus and spent the whole afternoon with Him.
Andrew was so convinced that he went straight to find his brother and told him, “We have found the Messiah.”
Then he brought Peter to Jesus.
John’s Gospel records the very first moment Jesus saw Peter.
Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon son of John.
You will be called Cephas.”
Cephas is the Aramaic word for “rock”; its Greek form is Petros, which gives us Peter.
Jesus named him before Peter had said or done anything at all.
That first meeting did not mean Peter left everything immediately.
For a while he seems to have kept fishing while spending time with Jesus.
The full call came later, on the shore of the lake, after a miraculous catch of fish (you’ll read about it below).
From then on, Peter left his boats and his business behind for good.
Why Jesus chose Peter.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why Jesus chose Peter.

What it does show is how Jesus chose His twelve apostles: Luke says He went up a mountain and spent the entire night praying to God, and in the morning He called His followers together and chose twelve of them.
Peter’s name is always first on the list.
It wasn’t because Peter was impressive.
Jesus could have chosen priests, scholars or wealthy men from Jerusalem.
Instead He chose fishermen, a tax collector and a political rebel from the backwater region of Galilee.
Paul later wrote that God deliberately chooses what the world thinks is foolish and weak, so that no one can boast.
What the Gospels do show is what Jesus saw in Peter.
When He named him “Rock,”
He was naming what He would make Peter become, not what Peter already was.
Peter was honest, wholehearted and willing to risk everything — he was the one who climbed out of the boat.
Jesus also knew Peter’s weaknesses better than Peter did; He predicted the denials before they happened and chose him anyway.
Peter’s story is the clearest picture in the Bible that Jesus calls people because of who He is, not because of who they already are.
A fisherman from Galilee.
Before he ever met Jesus, Peter’s life was the lake.
He and his brother Andrew lived in Capernaum, a town of perhaps 1,500 people built from black volcanic stone on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee.
Archaeologists have excavated a house there that has been honored as Peter’s house since the first century.
One room was turned into a meeting place for Christians very early, and an ancient church was later built right over it.
The fishing business was organized like a small company.
Peter and Andrew owned at least one boat and worked alongside James and John, whose father Zebedee had hired servants.
A first-century fishing boat discovered in the mud of the lake in 1986 is about 27 feet long and 7½ feet wide and could carry around a dozen people.
Fishermen worked through the night using dragnets and cast nets, sold their catch in the morning, and spent hours repairing torn nets.
Peter was married and his mother-in-law lived with the family.
One Sabbath, after Jesus taught in the Capernaum synagogue, He came to Peter’s house and found her sick in bed with a high fever.
He took her by the hand and helped her up, and the fever left her immediately — so completely that she got up and began serving them.
That evening, the whole town gathered at Peter’s door, and Jesus healed many who were sick.
Peter’s home became something like Jesus’ base in Galilee.
A new name.
In the Bible, names carry meaning.
When God gave someone a new name, it marked a new identity and a new calling: Abram became Abraham, “father of many”; Jacob became Israel, “he struggles with God.”
Jesus did the same thing with Peter at their very first meeting.
The new name — Cephas in Aramaic, Petros in Greek — means “rock” or “stone.”
It was not a normal name in that era; we don’t have clear examples of anyone else being called “Rock” before Peter.
So everyone who heard it would have asked why.
The irony is that Peter was anything but rock-steady.
He was impulsive and changeable, capable of great faith one moment and panic the next.
Jesus was not describing Peter’s personality — He was announcing what He was going to make of him.
Later, Jesus explained it more fully: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church.”
For the rest of the New Testament, Peter goes by several names: Simon, Simon Peter, Peter and Cephas.
Paul usually calls him Cephas.
Jesus Himself, at important moments, went back to his old name — “Simon, Simon,” or “Simon son of John” — often when Peter was falling short of who he was meant to be.
“Put out into deep water”.
One morning, crowds were pressing in on Jesus along the shore of the lake, so many that He couldn’t teach them.
He saw two boats pulled up on the beach while the fishermen washed their nets.
He climbed into the one that belonged to Peter and asked him to push out a little from shore, then sat down and taught the people from the boat.
Water carries sound well, and the shoreline made a natural amphitheater.
When He finished speaking, Jesus turned to Peter: “Put out into deep water, and let down the nets for a catch.”
Peter was the expert, and he knew this made no sense.
They had worked hard all night — the best time for fishing — and caught nothing.
Daytime fishing in deep water was the worst plan possible.
But Peter said, “Master, because You say so, I will let down the nets.”
They caught so many fish that the nets began to break.
They signaled to James and John in the other boat to come help, and they filled both boats so full that they began to sink.
Peter’s reaction is surprising.
He didn’t celebrate the biggest catch of his life.
He fell at Jesus’ knees and said, “Go away from me, Lord; I am a sinful man!”
In that moment he realized he was in the presence of someone holy, and he felt unworthy.
Jesus answered with words He would say many times: “Don’t be afraid.
From now on you will fish for people.”
So they pulled their boats up on shore, left everything — including the biggest catch they’d ever had — and followed Him.
Walking on water.
This happened right after Jesus fed more than 5,000 people with five loaves and two fish.
The crowd wanted to take Jesus by force and make Him king, so He immediately sent the disciples across the lake by boat, dismissed the crowd, and went up a mountain alone to pray.
By nightfall the boat was far from land, battered by waves because the wind was against them.
The disciples rowed for hours and made little progress.
Shortly before dawn — between three and six in the morning — they saw a figure walking toward them on the water.
They were terrified and screamed, “It’s a ghost!”
Jesus called out immediately: “Take courage! It is I. Don’t be afraid.”
And Peter, being Peter, answered, “Lord, if it’s You, tell me to come to You on the water.”
Jesus said one word: “Come.”
Peter climbed over the side of the boat and actually walked on the water toward Jesus.
He is the only human being in the Bible besides Jesus who ever did this.
But then he took his eyes off Jesus and noticed how strong the wind was.
He panicked and began to sink, crying out, “Lord, save me!”
Jesus immediately reached out His hand and caught him. “You of little faith,”
He said, “why did you doubt?”
When they climbed into the boat, the wind stopped.
The disciples worshiped Jesus and said, “Truly You are the Son of God.”
Peter is sometimes remembered for sinking — but he was the only one of the twelve who got out of the boat.
“You are the Messiah”.
About two and a half years into Jesus’ ministry, He took His disciples far north to the region of Caesarea Philippi, near the foot of Mount Hermon.
It was a pagan area full of shrines to the Greek god Pan and a temple honoring the Roman emperor as a god.
There Jesus asked them, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?”
They reported the rumors: some said John the Baptist come back to life, others Elijah, Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.
Then Jesus asked the question that mattered: “But what about you? Who do you say I am?”
Peter answered for all of them: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
Messiah (Christ in Greek) means “anointed one” — the King God had promised for centuries.
Jesus told Peter he was blessed, because no human had revealed this to him, but His Father in heaven.
Then He said, “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”
But the very next moment shows Peter’s other side.
Jesus began explaining that He must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day.
Peter took Him aside and actually began to scold Him: “Never, Lord!
This shall never happen to You!”
Jesus turned and said to him, “Get behind Me, Satan!
You are a stumbling block to Me; you do not have in mind the concerns of God, but merely human concerns.”
In the space of a few minutes, Peter went from speaking a truth revealed by God to repeating the devil’s temptation — to avoid the cross.
He believed Jesus was the Messiah, but he still expected a conquering king, not a suffering Savior.
On the mountain.
About a week after Peter’s confession, Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain by themselves.
These three were His inner circle — the only ones He brought into certain private moments.
While Jesus was praying, His appearance changed.
His face shone like the sun and His clothes became dazzling white, brighter than anyone on earth could bleach them.
Then Moses and Elijah appeared and talked with Him.
Luke adds that they were discussing His “departure” — His death — which was about to happen in Jerusalem.
Moses represented the Law and Elijah the Prophets; together they stood with Jesus as the one the whole Old Testament pointed to.
The disciples had been drowsy, but now they were wide awake and terrified.
Peter, not knowing what to say, blurted out, “Lord, it is good for us to be here.
Let us put up three shelters — one for You, one for Moses and one for Elijah.”
Perhaps he wanted to make the moment last, or treat all three as equals.
While he was still speaking, a bright cloud covered them and a voice came from the cloud: “This is My Son, whom I love; with Him I am well pleased. Listen to Him!”
The disciples fell face down in fear.
Then Jesus came and touched them: “Get up. Don’t be afraid.”
When they looked up, they saw only Jesus.
Peter never forgot it.

Some thirty years later he wrote: “We did not follow cleverly devised stories… we were eyewitnesses of His majesty… we ourselves heard this voice that came from heaven when we were with Him on the sacred mountain.”
The foot washing.
It was the night of the Passover meal, the last evening before Jesus died.
Peter and John had been sent ahead to prepare the meal in a large upstairs room in Jerusalem.
Luke records that the disciples even argued that night about which of them was the greatest.
In that world, people walked dusty roads in sandals, and washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest servant. No servant was there.
During the meal, Jesus got up, took off His outer robe, wrapped a towel around His waist, poured water into a basin, and began washing His disciples’ feet one by one.
When He came to Peter, Peter was horrified.
“Lord, are You going to wash my feet? … You shall never wash my feet.”
Jesus answered, “Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me.”
Peter swung completely to the opposite extreme: “Then, Lord, not just my feet but my hands and my head as well!”
Jesus explained that someone who has bathed only needs to wash his feet.
Afterward He told them, “I have set you an example that you should do as I have done for you.”
Later that evening Jesus warned them that they would all fall away that night.
Peter insisted, “Even if all fall away, I will not… Lord, I am ready to go with You to prison and to death.”
Jesus answered, “Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you as wheat.
But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith may not fail.
And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”
Then He told him plainly: “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny three times that you know Me.”
The sword in the garden.
After the meal they walked out of the city, across the Kidron Valley, to an olive grove called Gethsemane on the Mount of Olives.
Jesus took Peter, James and John further in and said, “My soul is overwhelmed with sorrow to the point of death.
Stay here and keep watch with Me.”
He went a little farther, fell to the ground and prayed, “Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from Me.
Yet not as I will, but as You will.”
When He came back, He found them asleep.
He said to Peter, “Couldn’t you keep watch with Me for one hour?
Watch and pray so that you will not fall into temptation.
The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.” It happened three times.
Then torches and lanterns appeared through the trees: a crowd sent by the chief priests, armed with swords and clubs, led by Judas.
Peter had a sword — the disciples had two between them — and he drew it and struck Malchus, the high priest’s servant, cutting off his right ear.
He may have been aiming for his head.
Jesus stopped it immediately: “Put your sword away!
Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?”
He reminded them He could call on more than twelve legions of angels if He wanted.
Then He touched the servant’s ear and healed him — His last miracle of healing before the cross, done for one of the men arresting Him.
The soldiers bound Jesus.
And every disciple, including Peter, ran away into the night.
Three denials.
Peter didn’t run far.
He followed the arresting party at a distance back into Jerusalem, to the house of the high priest, Caiaphas.
John, who knew the high priest, got Peter into the courtyard.
It was a cold night, and Peter stood with the guards and servants around a charcoal fire, warming himself, while Jesus was being questioned inside.
A servant girl at the gate looked closely at him in the firelight: “You also were with Jesus of Galilee.”
Peter denied it in front of everyone: “I don’t know what you’re talking about.”
A little later, another person said, “This fellow was with Jesus of Nazareth.”
Peter denied it again, this time with an oath: “I don’t know the man!”
About an hour later, some of those standing nearby came up to him.
One was a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter had cut off: “Didn’t I see you with Him in the olive grove?
Surely you are one of them — your accent gives you away.”
Peter began to call down curses on himself and swore, “I don’t know the man!”
Immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed.
Luke records something the others don’t: at that moment, Jesus — being led across the courtyard — turned and looked straight at Peter.
Peter remembered exactly what Jesus had said, went outside, and wept bitterly.
The man who promised to die for Jesus could not admit to a servant girl that he knew Him.
It was the lowest moment of his life.
Running to the tomb.
Peter was not at the cross.
Of the twelve, only John is mentioned there.
We don’t know where Peter spent Friday and Saturday, but we can imagine the grief and shame he carried.
Early on Sunday morning, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and found the stone rolled away.
She ran to Peter and John: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have put Him!”
The two men ran.
John was faster and got there first, but stopped at the entrance and only looked in.
Peter arrived and went straight inside.
He saw the strips of linen lying there, and the cloth that had been wrapped around Jesus’ head, folded up by itself, separate from the linen.
It didn’t look like a robbery — thieves wouldn’t unwrap a body and leave the expensive linen behind.
That same day, the risen Jesus appeared to Peter personally.
Luke records the disciples saying, “It is true!
The Lord has risen and has appeared to Simon.”
Paul lists it too: Jesus “appeared to Cephas, and then to the Twelve.”
The Bible never tells us what Jesus said to Peter in that private meeting.
“Do you love me?”.
Some time after Easter, seven of the disciples were back in Galilee by the lake.
Peter said, “I’m going out to fish,” and the others went with him.
They fished all night and caught nothing — just like the morning Jesus first called Peter.
At dawn a man stood on the shore and called out, “Friends, haven’t you any fish?” “No.”
“Throw your net on the right side of the boat and you will find some.”
They did, and the net was so full they couldn’t haul it in.
John said to Peter, “It is the Lord!”
Peter grabbed his outer garment, jumped into the water, and swam the hundred yards to shore.
The others followed, dragging a net with 153 large fish — and it didn’t tear.
Jesus had a charcoal fire burning with fish and bread on it, and He served them breakfast.
The only other charcoal fire in the Gospels is the one Peter stood beside when he denied Jesus.
After breakfast Jesus turned to him: “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?”
“Yes, Lord, You know that I love You.” “Feed My lambs.”
A second time: “Do you love Me?” “Yes, Lord.” “Take care of My sheep.”
A third time: “Do you love Me?”
Peter was hurt that Jesus asked a third time.
“Lord, You know all things; You know that I love You.” “Feed My sheep.”
Three denials, three declarations of love, three times being given a job.
Jesus didn’t just forgive Peter — He put him back to work leading His people.
Then He told Peter that when he was old, someone would stretch out his hands and lead him where he didn’t want to go — John explains this described the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God.
And Jesus ended with the same words He said on the beach at the beginning: “Follow Me.”
Pentecost.
Forty days after the resurrection, Jesus was taken up into heaven, telling the disciples to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit.
About 120 believers met together and prayed.
Peter took the lead in replacing Judas, and Matthias was chosen.
Ten days later came the Jewish festival of Pentecost, when Jerusalem was packed with Jewish pilgrims from all over the Roman world.
Suddenly a sound like a violent wind filled the house where the disciples were, and what looked like tongues of fire came to rest on each of them.
They were filled with the Holy Spirit and began speaking in other languages.
A crowd gathered, amazed that these Galileans were speaking in the native languages of visitors from Persia, Egypt, Rome, Arabia and more.
Some mocked: “They’ve had too much wine.”
Peter stood up with the other eleven and raised his voice.
“These people are not drunk — it’s only nine in the morning!”
This, he said, was what the prophet Joel had promised: God pouring out His Spirit on all people.
Then he preached about Jesus: a man accredited by God through miracles, handed over to be killed — “and you, with the help of wicked men, put Him to death by nailing Him to the cross.
But God raised Him from the dead.”
He quoted David’s psalms and declared, “God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Messiah.”
The crowd was cut to the heart and asked, “What shall we do?”
Peter answered, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins.
And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”
About 3,000 people were baptized that day.
Seven weeks earlier, Peter had been too scared to admit he knew Jesus to a servant girl.
Now he was accusing the city of crucifying its Messiah, in public, a few hundred yards from where it happened.
Healing and courage.
One afternoon Peter and John were going up to the Temple for the three o’clock prayer.
At the gate called Beautiful sat a man who had been unable to walk since birth — over forty years old — carried there every day to beg. He asked them for money.
Peter looked straight at him and said, “Look at us!”
The man looked up, expecting coins.
Peter said, “Silver or gold I do not have, but what I do have I give you.
In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.”
He took him by the right hand and helped him up, and instantly his feet and ankles became strong.
The man jumped up and went into the Temple with them, walking and jumping and praising God.
A crowd came running, and Peter preached again: “Why does this surprise you?
It is not by our own power.
It is faith in the name of Jesus that has made this man strong.” Thousands more believed.
The priests and Temple guards arrested Peter and John and kept them overnight.
The next morning they stood before the same council that had condemned Jesus — including Annas and Caiaphas.
“By what power or what name did you do this?”
Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said it was by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised.
“Salvation is found in no one else.”
The council was astonished at the courage of these unschooled, ordinary men, and they recognized they had been with Jesus.
They couldn’t deny the miracle — the healed man was standing right there.
They ordered them never to speak or teach in the name of Jesus.
Peter and John replied, “Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to Him? You be the judges!
As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
Later all the apostles were arrested and flogged.
They left rejoicing that they had been counted worthy of suffering disgrace for the Name.
Crowds even brought the sick into the streets hoping Peter’s shadow would fall on them as he passed.
The door opened to everyone.
In the early years, nearly all the believers were Jewish.
Jews kept God’s food laws and generally did not eat with or enter the homes of Gentiles (non-Jews).
Many assumed that to follow the Messiah, a Gentile would first have to become Jewish.
In the coastal city of Caesarea lived a Roman army officer named Cornelius, a centurion who worshiped God, gave generously to the poor and prayed regularly.
An angel told him to send men to Joppa to bring back a man named Peter.
The next day around noon, Peter went up on the flat roof of the house where he was staying to pray.
He got hungry, and while lunch was being prepared he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven open and something like a large sheet let down by its four corners, full of all kinds of animals, reptiles and birds — many forbidden by Jewish law.
A voice said, “Get up, Peter. Kill and eat.” “Surely not, Lord!
I have never eaten anything impure or unclean.”
The voice said, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean.”
This happened three times.
While Peter was puzzling over it, Cornelius’s men arrived at the gate.
The Spirit told Peter to go with them.

In Caesarea, Peter walked into a Gentile home full of Cornelius’s relatives and friends, and said, “I now realize how true it is that God does not show favoritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears Him and does what is right.”
While Peter was still speaking about Jesus, the Holy Spirit came on everyone listening, and they began speaking in tongues and praising God, exactly as the apostles had at Pentecost.
Peter said, “Surely no one can stand in the way of their being baptized with water.”
He later defended this before the church in Jerusalem, and it became one of the most important turning points in history: the message of Jesus was for the whole world.
Freed by an angel.
Around AD 44, King Herod Agrippa I — grandson of the Herod who tried to kill baby Jesus — began persecuting the church to win popularity.
He had James, the brother of John, executed with the sword.
When he saw that this pleased the Jewish leaders, he arrested Peter too, during the Passover festival, planning to put him on public trial afterward.
Peter was guarded by four squads of four soldiers each.
Meanwhile, the church was praying earnestly to God for him.
The night before his trial, Peter was asleep — sleeping, the night before his likely execution — chained between two soldiers, with guards at the door.
Suddenly an angel appeared and a light shone in the cell.
The angel struck Peter on the side and woke him: “Quick, get up!”
The chains fell off his wrists.
“Put on your clothes and sandals… wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”
Peter followed, thinking he was seeing a vision.
They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading into the city.
It opened for them by itself.
They walked one street, and the angel was gone.
Peter came to himself and said, “Now I know without a doubt that the Lord has rescued me.”
He went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many people were gathered praying.
He knocked at the outer door.
A servant girl named Rhoda recognized his voice and was so overjoyed she ran back in without opening the door. “Peter is at the door!”
“You’re out of your mind,” they told her. “It must be his angel.” Peter kept knocking.
When they finally opened the door, they were astonished.
Peter told them what happened, asked them to tell James (the brother of Jesus), and then left for another place.
Herod, after executing the guards, went to Caesarea, where shortly afterward he was struck down and died.
How it ended.
After his escape, Peter appears only briefly in Acts.

At the Council of Jerusalem (about AD 49) he stood up and argued that Gentile believers should not be burdened with the Jewish law: “We believe it is through the grace of our Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

Paul’s letters mention him traveling with his wife and ministering in places like Antioch, where Paul once confronted him publicly for withdrawing from eating with Gentile Christians — Peter still had his inconsistent moments.
Peter wrote two letters in the New Testament, 1 and 2 Peter, to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey who were facing hostility and persecution.
They are full of hope: “Cast all your anxiety on Him because He cares for you.”
“Your enemy the devil prowls around like a roaring lion.”
He calls himself “a witness of Christ’s sufferings.”
He mentions writing from “Babylon,” which early Christians commonly used as a code name for Rome.
The earliest traditions also say that the Gospel of Mark was based on Peter’s preaching, which Mark wrote down.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly how Peter died, but Jesus had told him he would stretch out his hands and be led where he did not want to go.
Clement of Rome, writing around AD 95, mentions Peter’s martyrdom.

Later writers including Tertullian and Eusebius say he was crucified in Rome during Emperor Nero’s persecution, around AD 64–67, and tradition has said he asked to be crucified upside down, not feeling worthy to die the same way as his Lord.
St.
Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City stands over the site traditionally honored as his grave.
Excavations under the church in the 1940s–50s uncovered a first-century cemetery and an early shrine at that spot.
What made Peter extraordinary.
Peter is named in the Gospels more than any other disciple.

He was the first to declare Jesus the Messiah, one of only three present at the Transfiguration and in the garden, the only disciple who walked on water, the first apostle to see the risen Jesus, the preacher of the first Christian sermon, the man God used to open the church to non-Jews, and a person whose shadow people hoped would heal them.
He also failed more publicly than almost anyone in the Bible: rebuked as “Satan,” sinking in the waves, sleeping in the garden, swinging a sword, and denying Jesus three times.
His story is told honestly, with no attempt to hide his worst moments — likely because Peter himself told them.
Why Peter matters today.
Peter shows that Jesus calls ordinary people, sees who they can become before they do, and doesn’t give up on them when they fail.
The night Peter denied Jesus could have been the end of his story, the way it was for Judas.
Instead, Jesus came looking for him, asked him three times, “Do you love Me?”, and handed him the job of caring for His people.
The fearful fisherman became the bold Rock.

As Peter himself wrote near the end of his life: “The God of all grace, who called you to His eternal glory in Christ, after you have suffered a little while, will Himself restore you and make you strong, firm and steadfast.”
Who Andrew was.
Andrew was Peter’s brother, and like Peter he was a fisherman from Bethsaida on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee who later lived in Capernaum.
His name is Greek, meaning “manly” or “brave” — a sign that Galilee was a crossroads where Jewish families often used Greek names.
Andrew was a seeker.
Before he ever met Jesus, he had made the long trip south to the Jordan River to follow John the Baptist, who was calling Israel to repent because the Messiah was coming.
That tells us Andrew was spiritually hungry and paying attention, waiting for God to act.
How Andrew met Jesus.
Andrew was standing with John the Baptist when Jesus walked by, and John said, “Look, the Lamb of God!”
Andrew and another disciple (probably John, son of Zebedee) immediately started following Jesus.
Jesus turned around and asked them the first question He asks in John’s Gospel: “What are you looking for?”
They asked where He was staying, and He said, “Come and see.”
They spent the rest of the day with Him — John even remembers it was about four in the afternoon.
That makes Andrew one of the first two people ever to follow Jesus.
And his very first act as a follower was to go and find his brother and bring him to Jesus.
Why Jesus chose Andrew.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why Jesus chose Andrew, but it shows us what kind of man he was.
Andrew had already left home to follow a prophet because he wanted God.
He recognized Jesus quickly and acted on it.
And every time he appears in John’s Gospel, he is bringing someone else to Jesus: his brother Peter, a boy with a small lunch, and a group of Greek visitors.
Jesus called His first disciples to become “fishers of people” — and Andrew was doing it before he was even asked.
Andrew was officially called by the lake, together with Peter, when Jesus walked by their boat and said, “Come, follow Me, and I will make you fishers of people.”
At once they left their nets.
He was part of Jesus’ circle of four (Peter, Andrew, James and John) and was with them on the Mount of Olives when Jesus spoke about the end of the age.
A seeker.
Andrew and his older brother Peter grew up in Bethsaida, a fishing village where the Jordan River flows into the north end of the Sea of Galilee.
The name Bethsaida means “house of fishing.”
Later the brothers shared a house in Capernaum, a few miles west.
But Andrew wasn’t content just to fish.
Around AD 27–28, news spread through Galilee about a prophet preaching in the wilderness near the Jordan River, about 70 miles south.

John the Baptist dressed like the ancient prophet Elijah and told everyone — even religious leaders and soldiers — to turn from their sins and be baptized, because God’s promised King was about to appear.
Andrew made that long journey and became one of John’s disciples.
That meant listening to John’s teaching, fasting and praying as he taught, and watching for the Messiah.
It tells us something important about Andrew: he was spiritually hungry.
He wasn’t satisfied with ordinary religion; he wanted God to act, and he was willing to leave home and work to be ready when He did.
The first to follow.
One day John the Baptist was standing by the Jordan with two of his disciples, Andrew and another man the Gospel doesn’t name (very likely John, son of Zebedee, who wrote that Gospel).
Jesus walked by, and John the Baptist said, “Look, the Lamb of God!”
To a Jewish listener, “lamb of God” would bring to mind the Passover lamb whose blood saved Israel in Egypt, and the lambs sacrificed every day at the Temple for sin.
The day before, John had said even more plainly: “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
Andrew didn’t wait.
He and his friend left John and started walking after Jesus.
Jesus turned around and asked them, “What do you want?” — or more literally, “What are you seeking?”
They answered, “Rabbi, where are You staying?”
It was a polite way of asking to spend time with Him.
Jesus said, “Come, and you will see.”
They went with Him and stayed the rest of the day.
John’s Gospel even remembers the time — “about the tenth hour,” around four in the afternoon.
Whatever Jesus said in those hours, Andrew walked away convinced he had found the one he had been waiting for.
He became, with his friend, one of the first two people in history to follow Jesus.
“We found the Messiah!”.
John’s Gospel says that the very first thing Andrew did was find his own brother.
He told him, “We have found the Messiah” — the anointed King promised by the prophets.
Then he brought him to Jesus.
Jesus looked at Andrew’s brother and gave him a new name: Cephas, or Peter, meaning “rock.”
From that moment Peter would become the leader of the apostles, the preacher at Pentecost and one of the most famous people in history — but it began with Andrew taking his brother by the arm.
Some time later, back in Galilee, Jesus officially called both brothers.
He walked along the shore and saw them casting a net into the lake. “Come, follow Me,”
Jesus said, “and I will send you out to fish for people.”
At once they left their nets and followed Him.

Andrew was also part of the small group Jesus sometimes took aside — Peter, Andrew, James and John — and was one of the four who asked Jesus privately on the Mount of Olives about the destruction of the Temple and the end of the age.
Andrew is never shown preaching to crowds.
He is shown doing something just as important: making introductions.
The boy’s lunch.
Huge crowds had followed Jesus to a remote hillside near the Sea of Galilee, close to Andrew’s hometown of Bethsaida. It was nearly Passover.
As evening came, there were about 5,000 men there, plus women and children, and nothing to eat.
Jesus asked Philip, “Where shall we buy bread for these people to eat?”
Philip calculated that even eight months of wages wouldn’t buy enough for each person to have a bite.
Andrew had been doing something different: looking at what they actually had.
He came to Jesus and said, “Here is a boy with five small barley loaves and two small fish.”
Barley bread was the cheap bread of the poor, and the fish were probably small, dried or pickled.
Then Andrew added his own honest doubt: “But how far will they go among so many?”
Jesus told everyone to sit down on the grass.
He took the loaves, gave thanks, and handed them out, and did the same with the fish — as much as anyone wanted.
When everyone was full, Jesus told the disciples to gather the leftovers so nothing would be wasted, and they filled twelve baskets.
The people said, “Surely this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.”
Andrew didn’t understand how a child’s lunch could help.
But he brought it to Jesus anyway — and that was enough.
Bringing the Greeks.
In Jesus’ final week, Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims for Passover.
Among them were some Greeks — Gentiles who worshiped the God of Israel.
They came to Philip, who also had a Greek name and was from Bethsaida, and asked, “Sir, we would like to see Jesus.”
Philip wasn’t sure what to do.
Jesus had mostly focused His ministry on Israel.
So Philip went to Andrew — and together Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.
Jesus’ response was striking.
“The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified,” He said.
“Unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a single seed.
But if it dies, it produces many seeds.”
Jesus was saying that His death was about to happen, and through it people from every nation would come to Him.
The arrival of these Greeks was a sign of the worldwide harvest to come.
It is the third time John’s Gospel shows Andrew bringing someone to Jesus: his brother, a boy with a lunch, and now foreigners.
Andrew seems to have understood early that Jesus was for everyone.
How it ended.
After Jesus rose from the dead and ascended to heaven, Andrew was with the other apostles in the upper room in Jerusalem, praying, when the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost.
That is the last time the Bible names him.
The Bible doesn’t say what happened to Andrew after that, but tradition has said a great deal.
The early church historian Eusebius, around AD 300, recorded that Andrew preached in Scythia — the region around the Black Sea, in parts of modern Ukraine, Romania and Russia.
That’s why he is honored as a patron saint of Ukraine, Romania and Russia.
Tradition has also said that he preached in Greece and was crucified at Patras around AD 60 by the Roman governor.

According to that account, Andrew asked to be crucified on an X-shaped cross rather than an upright one like Jesus’, and he was tied rather than nailed so that he would suffer longer — and he preached to the crowd from the cross for two days until he died.
The X-shaped cross, called the saltire or St.
Andrew’s Cross, became his symbol.
It forms the flag of Scotland, which adopted Andrew as its patron saint after legends that some of his relics were brought there.
His feast day is November 30.
Why Andrew matters today.
Andrew lived in his famous brother’s shadow.
Peter preached to thousands; Andrew is barely quoted.
But Peter was there because Andrew brought him.
Andrew shows that one of the most important things anyone can do is quietly bring another person to Jesus — and then step back and let Jesus do the rest.
Who James was.
James was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee, the son of Zebedee and the older brother of John.
Zebedee ran a fishing business large enough to employ hired workers, so the family was reasonably well-off.
Their mother, likely named Salome, later followed Jesus too, supporting Him and standing near the cross when He died.
Some scholars think she was a sister of Mary, which would make James and John cousins of Jesus — but the Bible doesn’t say that directly.
He is often called “James the Greater” to tell him apart from the other apostle named James, the son of Alphaeus.
How James met Jesus.
James and John were partners with Peter and Andrew.
After the miraculous catch of fish, when Peter’s boat nearly sank, James and John were there too, amazed.
Jesus walked along the shore and saw the two brothers in a boat with their father, preparing their nets.
He called them, and immediately they left the boat and their father and followed Him.
Mark adds the small, human detail that they left Zebedee “in the boat with the hired men.”
Why Jesus chose James.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why Jesus chose James, but it shows he was wholehearted and fierce.
Jesus nicknamed him and John “Boanerges,” meaning “Sons of Thunder” — most likely because of their fiery tempers and intense loyalty.
Jesus didn’t choose them because they were gentle; He chose them and then taught them what real greatness looks like.
James became one of the three disciples closest to Jesus.
Leaving the boat.
James and his younger brother John worked in their father Zebedee’s fishing business on the Sea of Galilee, in partnership with Peter and Andrew.
Zebedee employed hired men, so the business was successful.
Their mother, probably named Salome, would later follow Jesus too.
James was there the morning of the miraculous catch, when Peter’s nets nearly broke and the partners’ boats almost sank.
Soon after, Jesus walked along the shore and saw James and John in a boat with their father, preparing their nets.
He called them, and immediately they left the boat and their father and followed Him.
Mark adds the detail that they left Zebedee “in the boat with the hired men” — the business would go on, but the sons were gone.
James is always named before John in the lists, likely because he was older.
Sons of Thunder.
When Jesus named His twelve apostles, He gave James and John a nickname: Boanerges, which Mark translates as “Sons of Thunder.” The Gospels show why.
As Jesus set out on His final journey to Jerusalem, He sent messengers ahead into a Samaritan village to get things ready.
Jews and Samaritans had a long, bitter hostility, and the village refused to welcome Him because He was heading to Jerusalem.
James and John were furious.
They asked, “Lord, do You want us to call fire down from heaven to destroy them?” — just as the prophet Elijah once did.
Jesus turned and rebuked them, and they went on to another village.
James and John were fiercely loyal and passionate, but they had to learn that Jesus came to save people, not destroy them.
The inner circle.
Out of the twelve, Jesus chose three — Peter, James and John — to be with Him at three of the most important moments of His ministry.

First, when a synagogue leader named Jairus begged Jesus to heal his dying 12-year-old daughter, and she died before they arrived, Jesus let no one follow Him into the house except Peter, James and John and the girl’s parents.
They watched Him take her hand and say, “Talitha koum” — “Little girl, get up” — and she stood up.
Second, Jesus took the three up a high mountain, where they saw Him transfigured, shining like the sun, talking with Moses and Elijah, and heard God’s voice from the cloud.
Third, on the night He was betrayed, Jesus took the same three deeper into the garden of Gethsemane and asked them to stay awake and pray while He agonized over the cross.
James saw Jesus’ greatest glory and His deepest suffering.
Asking for the best seats.

On the road to Jerusalem, right after Jesus told the twelve for the third time that He would be mocked, flogged and killed and rise again, James and John came to Him with a request. (Matthew says their mother came with them and knelt to ask.) “Teacher, we want You to do for us whatever we ask… Let one of us sit at Your right and the other at Your left in Your glory.”
They still imagined Jesus would set up an earthly throne, and they wanted the top two positions.
Jesus said, “You don’t know what you are asking.
Can you drink the cup I drink or be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with?”
They answered confidently, “We can.”
Jesus told them, “You will drink the cup I drink” — they would share in His suffering — but the places of honor were not His to grant.
When the other ten heard about it, they were angry with the brothers.
So Jesus called them all together and said: among the rulers of this world, the powerful lord it over others. “Not so with you.
Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant… For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
The first apostle to die.
After Pentecost, James was one of the leaders of the church in Jerusalem.
About eleven years after the resurrection, King Herod Agrippa I — grandson of Herod the Great — began arresting believers to please the religious leaders.
Acts records it in a single verse: Herod “had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword.”
James became the first of the twelve apostles to die for his faith — the only apostle whose death is recorded in the Bible.
Years before, he had told Jesus he could drink His cup, and Jesus had told him he would. He did.

Eusebius preserves a story from Clement of Alexandria that the man who brought James to trial was so moved by his testimony that he declared himself a Christian too, and the two were executed together.
The Bible doesn’t say where James was buried, but Spanish tradition has said his remains were carried to Spain and rest at Santiago de Compostela — “St.
James of the field of the star” — the destination of the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage, walked by hundreds of thousands of people every year.
Why James matters today.
James asked for a throne and was given a cup of suffering instead — and he drank it faithfully, as the first of the twelve to die for Jesus.
His story reminds us that following Jesus is not about status but about faithfulness, even to the end.
Who John was.
John was the younger brother of James and the son of Zebedee, a fisherman with a family business on the Sea of Galilee.
He was probably the youngest of the twelve apostles, perhaps still a teenager or in his early twenties when he started following Jesus.
He is one of the most important people in the New Testament.
John wrote (or is traditionally credited with) five books: the Gospel of John, the letters 1, 2 and 3 John, and the Book of Revelation.
Interestingly, in his own Gospel he never once uses his own name.
He calls himself “the disciple whom Jesus loved.”
How John met Jesus.
John’s Gospel tells of two disciples of John the Baptist who first followed Jesus.
One was Andrew; the other is unnamed, and many believe it was John himself, writing modestly.
Later, Jesus called John and his brother James from their father’s boat, and they left immediately to follow Him.
Why Jesus chose John.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why Jesus chose John, but it shows a young man with intense passion.
Jesus nicknamed him and James “Sons of Thunder.”
John once tried to stop a stranger from driving out demons in Jesus’ name because he “wasn’t one of us,” and he wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.
Jesus took that fierce loyalty and, over a lifetime, turned it into love.
The man who wanted to burn a village became the apostle who wrote “God is love.”
John was part of the inner three, present at the raising of Jairus’s daughter, the Transfiguration, and in Gethsemane.
A young fisherman.
John was probably the youngest of the twelve.
He may be the unnamed disciple who, with Andrew, first followed Jesus after John the Baptist pointed Him out.
In his own Gospel he never uses his name, calling himself “the disciple whom Jesus loved.”
A Son of Thunder.
John told Jesus, “We saw someone driving out demons in Your name and we told him to stop, because he wasn’t one of us.”
Jesus said, “Don’t stop him.
Whoever is not against us is for us.”
The same man who later wrote “God is love” started out with a hot temper.
Close to Jesus.
Jesus announced that one of the twelve would betray Him.
Peter motioned to John, who was leaning against Jesus, to ask who.
Jesus said it was the one to whom He would give a piece of bread dipped in the dish — and handed it to Judas.
John was with Peter and James in Gethsemane, and later got into the high priest’s courtyard because he knew the high priest.
At the cross.
Standing near the cross were Mary the mother of Jesus, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, Mary Magdalene — and John.
Dying, Jesus saw His mother and John and said to her, “Woman, here is your son,” and to John, “Here is your mother.”
From that hour John took her into his home.
John also records details only an eyewitness would note: the soldiers gambling for the seamless robe, and blood and water flowing from Jesus’ side.
He saw and believed.
When Mary Magdalene reported the tomb empty, John and Peter ran.
John arrived first, looked in and saw the linen lying there, but waited.
After Peter went in, John went in too, and “he saw and believed.”
A week later by the lake, it was John who first recognized the stranger on the shore: “It is the Lord!”
A pillar of the church.
John and Peter were arrested together for preaching about Jesus.
When the gospel spread to Samaria, the apostles sent Peter and John to pray for the new believers.
Paul later called James (the brother of Jesus), Peter and John the “pillars” of the Jerusalem church.
God is love.
John’s Gospel opens, “In the beginning was the Word… and the Word became flesh,” and includes “For God so loved the world that He gave His only Son.”
His first letter says, “God is love.
Whoever lives in love lives in God.”
He wrote so that readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name.
Exile on Patmos.
The writer of Revelation calls himself John, a brother and companion in suffering, on Patmos “because of the word of God.”
There he saw the risen Christ in blinding glory and was shown visions of heaven and the end of the age, ending with a new heaven and new earth where God wipes away every tear.
Early writers say John lived to a very old age in Ephesus, the only apostle not killed for his faith.
Jerome records that, when he was too frail to preach, he would only say: “Little children, love one another.”
What made John extraordinary.

John was the only one of the twelve who stood at the cross, the one Jesus trusted with His own mother, the first to believe at the empty tomb, the first to recognize the risen Jesus by the lake, and the one who received the visions of Revelation.
He outlived all the other apostles.
Why John matters today.
John’s life shows how Jesus can transform a person over time.
He began as a “Son of Thunder” and ended as the apostle of love.
His Gospel was written, he says, “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.”
Who Philip was.
Philip came from Bethsaida, the same fishing town as Peter and Andrew.
His name is Greek (“lover of horses”), which may be why later some Greek visitors in Jerusalem came to him first when they wanted to see Jesus.
Philip appears only a few times in the Gospels, almost all in John’s Gospel, and he comes across as practical, analytical and honest.
How Philip met Jesus.
The day after Andrew and Peter met Jesus, Jesus decided to go to Galilee.
He found Philip and said simply, “Follow Me.”
Philip is one of the few people whom Jesus actively sought out rather than being brought by someone else.
Philip immediately went and found his friend Nathanael and told him, “We have found the one Moses wrote about in the Law, and about whom the prophets also wrote — Jesus of Nazareth.”
Why Jesus chose Philip.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why Jesus chose Philip.
What we see is a man who believed quickly and invited others without arguing — “Come and see.”
We also see Jesus patiently stretching him: testing him before feeding the 5,000, and gently answering his request at the Last Supper to “show us the Father.”
Philip shows that Jesus chooses careful, practical thinkers too, and grows their faith beyond their calculations.
“Follow me”.
Philip is a Greek name, which may explain why Greek visitors later came to him first.
John’s Gospel is the only one that tells us much about him.
Come and see.
Philip said, “We have found the one Moses wrote about in the Law, and the prophets also wrote about — Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”
Nathanael said, “Nazareth!
Can anything good come from there?” Philip didn’t argue.
He just invited him to meet Jesus for himself.
The impossible math.
John says Jesus asked only to test him; He already knew what He would do.
Philip calculated that 200 denarii — about eight months of a laborer’s pay — wouldn’t buy enough for each person to get a bite.
Then Jesus fed the whole crowd with five loaves and two fish.
“Show us the Father”.
Jesus had just said, “I am the way, the truth and the life.
No one comes to the Father except through Me.”
Philip asked to see the Father.
Jesus replied, “Don’t you know Me, Philip, even after I have been among you such a long time?
Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father.”
How it ended.
Don’t confuse him with Philip the evangelist in Acts 8, a different man who was one of the seven deacons and baptized the Ethiopian official.
Second-century writers say the apostle Philip died at Hierapolis in what is now Turkey.
Archaeologists there have excavated a church built in his honor.
Why Philip matters today.
Philip’s “Come and see” is still one of the best ways to share faith: not winning an argument, but inviting someone to meet Jesus for themselves.
Who Bartholomew was.
Bartholomew appears in every list of the twelve apostles, but the first three Gospels tell us nothing else about him.
His name is actually a family name: “Bar-Tolmai,” son of Tolmai.
John’s Gospel never mentions Bartholomew, but tells a detailed story about a man named Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, a friend of Philip.
Because Bartholomew is always listed right beside Philip, most scholars believe Nathanael Bar-Tolmai is one person.
How he met Jesus.
His friend Philip came to him excited: “We have found the Messiah — Jesus of Nazareth.”
Nathanael was skeptical: “Nazareth!
Can anything good come from there?”
Philip said, “Come and see.”
As Nathanael approached, Jesus said, “Here truly is an Israelite in whom there is no deceit.”
Surprised, Nathanael asked how He knew him.
Jesus answered, “I saw you while you were still under the fig tree before Philip called you.”
Something about that detail — perhaps a private moment of prayer — overwhelmed him, and he declared, “Rabbi, You are the Son of God; You are the King of Israel.”
Why Jesus chose him.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why, but Jesus’ first words describe him: a man with nothing false about him.
Nathanael said exactly what he thought, even when it was rude.
Jesus valued that honesty, met his skepticism with a personal sign, and promised him he would see far greater things — heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man.
Two names, one man.
Bartholomew means “son of Tolmai” — a family name.
Matthew, Mark and Luke always pair him with Philip; John never mentions Bartholomew but tells the story of Philip’s friend Nathanael (“gift of God”) from Cana.
Putting those together, he is likely Nathanael Bar-Tolmai.
“Anything good from Nazareth?”.
Nazareth had maybe a few hundred people and is never mentioned in the Old Testament.
Nathanael was from Cana, a nearby town, so it might even have been a bit of local rivalry. He said what he thought.
Under the fig tree.
Something about that detail stunned Nathanael — perhaps he had been praying there alone.
He went from skeptic to believer in a moment: “Rabbi, You are the Son of God!
You are the King of Israel!”
Jesus told him he would see greater things: heaven opened and angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man — echoing Jacob’s ladder.
How it ended.
Nathanael is named among those fishing with Peter when Jesus appeared on the shore and cooked them breakfast.
Early church historian Eusebius reports he took the Gospel of Matthew to India.
Armenian tradition has said he was martyred there.
He is often shown in art holding a knife, from the tradition that he was flayed.
Why he matters today.
Bartholomew shows that honest doubt isn’t a barrier to Jesus.
Jesus knew him before they met and welcomed his questions.
Who Thomas was.

Thomas was one of the twelve apostles, also called Didymus, which is Greek for “twin.” (Thomas comes from the Aramaic word for twin too.) The Bible never tells us who his twin was, where he came from, or what work he did before following Jesus, though he was among the disciples who went fishing in Galilee after the resurrection, so he may have been a fisherman.
How Thomas met Jesus.
The Gospels don’t record Thomas’s calling.
He simply appears in the list of twelve whom Jesus chose after a night of prayer.
Everything we know about his personality comes from four short scenes in John’s Gospel — and in each one, Thomas says exactly what he thinks.
Why Jesus chose Thomas.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why Jesus chose Thomas, but his story shows a loyal, brave, blunt man who wanted real answers.
He was willing to die with Jesus, he asked the honest questions others were afraid to ask, and when he finally saw the risen Jesus, he made the clearest declaration of Jesus’ divinity in the Gospels.
Jesus didn’t reject Thomas for doubting — He came back specifically for him.
The Twin.
Thomas is a Greek form of the Aramaic word for “twin,” and John’s Gospel adds his Greek nickname, Didymus, which also means twin.
The Bible never tells us who his twin was, where he was from, or what his work was.
He was among the seven disciples fishing on the Sea of Galilee after the resurrection, so he may have been a fisherman from Galilee like several others.
Matthew, Mark and Luke only mention Thomas in their lists of the twelve.
Almost everything we know about his personality comes from four short scenes in John’s Gospel.
In every one, Thomas speaks his mind honestly — whether it’s courage, confusion, or doubt.
“Let us die with Him”.
Not long before His death, Jesus had been teaching in Jerusalem during a winter festival, and the religious leaders picked up stones to kill Him for claiming to be one with God.
Jesus withdrew across the Jordan River to safety.
Then a message came from Bethany, a village just two miles from Jerusalem: Jesus’ close friend Lazarus was sick.
Jesus waited two days, then said, “Let us go back to Judea.”
The disciples were alarmed: “Rabbi, a short while ago the Jews there tried to stone You, and yet You are going back?”
Jesus told them plainly that Lazarus had died, and that He was going to wake him.
It was Thomas who spoke up to the rest of the group: “Let us also go, that we may die with Him.”
It sounds gloomy, maybe even fatalistic — Thomas didn’t expect it to end well.
But it was also brave and loyal.
He believed going back meant death, and he was willing to go anyway.
“Doubting Thomas” was, first, Courageous Thomas.
“How can we know the way?”.
At the Last Supper, Jesus began preparing His disciples for His death.
He told them not to let their hearts be troubled: “My Father’s house has many rooms… I am going there to prepare a place for you… I will come back and take you to be with Me.”
Then He added, “You know the way to the place where I am going.”
Thomas didn’t pretend to understand.
“Lord, we don’t know where You are going, so how can we know the way?”
His honest confusion drew out one of the most famous sayings in the Bible.
Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life.
No one comes to the Father except through Me.
If you really know Me, you will know My Father as well.”
Thomas wanted a map. Jesus gave him a person.
If Thomas had nodded along like the others, that sentence might never have been spoken.
The doubt.
On the evening of the first Easter Sunday, the disciples were together behind locked doors, afraid of the religious leaders.
Suddenly Jesus stood among them and said, “Peace be with you!”
He showed them His hands and His side, and they were overjoyed.
But Thomas wasn’t there.
The Bible doesn’t say why.
When the others told him, “We have seen the Lord!”
Thomas refused to accept it secondhand.
He had watched Jesus be crucified.
He knew dead men don’t come back.
He said, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands and put my finger where the nails were, and put my hand into His side, I will not believe.”
It’s easy to criticize Thomas, but notice what he asked for: the same evidence the others had already received.
And he stayed with the group for the next week, still in the room, still waiting.
“My Lord and my God!”.
Eight days later, the disciples were in the house again, and this time Thomas was with them.
The doors were locked, but Jesus came and stood among them: “Peace be with you!”
Then He turned straight to Thomas.
Jesus quoted Thomas’s own words back to him — He had heard every one.
“Put your finger here; see My hands.
Reach out your hand and put it into My side.
Stop doubting and believe.”
The Bible doesn’t say whether Thomas actually touched the wounds.
It only records what he said: “My Lord and my God!”
It is the clearest, most complete statement of who Jesus is anywhere in the Gospels — not just Teacher, not just Messiah, but Lord and God.
Jesus answered, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
That blessing was for every future believer — including everyone reading this today.
John then explains why he wrote his Gospel: so that you may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and by believing have life in His name.
How it ended.
Thomas appears once more in the Bible: fishing with Peter and others on the Sea of Galilee when the risen Jesus appeared on the shore.
After that, he is listed among the apostles praying in Jerusalem before Pentecost.
The Bible doesn’t say what happened to Thomas after that, but tradition has said he traveled farther than any other apostle.
Early writings say he preached in Parthia (modern Iran) and then sailed to India. The St.
Thomas Christians of Kerala, in southwest India, have said for centuries that he landed on the Malabar Coast in AD 52 and founded seven churches.
Their community is one of the oldest Christian communities in the world.
Tradition has said that Thomas was killed with a spear around AD 72 at a hill near Mylapore, in today’s city of Chennai.
The San Thome Basilica in Chennai stands over his traditional tomb, and the hill is now called St. Thomas Mount.
The disciple remembered for doubting is said to have carried his faith to the far edge of the known world.
Why Thomas matters today.
He’s remembered as “Doubting Thomas,” but his story ends with faith, not doubt.
Jesus meets honest questions with evidence and invitation: “Touch and see.”
And Jesus added a blessing for everyone who came after: “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
Who Matthew was.
Matthew, also called Levi son of Alphaeus, was a tax collector in Capernaum, the lakeside town where Peter lived.
He worked for Herod Antipas, who ruled Galilee under Rome.
His booth was likely on the busy trade road along the lake, collecting tolls and customs on goods and fish.
Tax collectors were among the most despised people in Jewish society.
They worked for foreign rulers and usually got rich by charging more than required and keeping the difference.
Religious Jews considered them traitors and lumped them together with prostitutes and “sinners.”
Because Matthew handled money and records, he would have been literate and organized — skills that later suited a Gospel writer.
How Matthew met Jesus.
Jesus had been teaching and healing all around Capernaum, so Matthew surely knew about Him.
One day Jesus walked past the tax booth, looked at Matthew, and said, “Follow Me.”
Matthew got up, left everything, and followed Him.
For a fisherman, quitting was temporary — the boats would still be there.
For Matthew, walking away from the tax booth meant losing his job and income for good.
Why Jesus chose Matthew.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why, but Jesus explained His reason for spending time with people like Matthew: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
By choosing a hated tax collector to be one of His closest friends, Jesus showed that no one was beyond His reach.
And He placed Matthew on the same team as Simon the Zealot, who hated Rome — a picture of how Jesus brings enemies together.
A hated job.
Capernaum sat on the international road known as the Way of the Sea, connecting Egypt with Damascus.
Goods passing through, and fish sold from the lake, were taxed.
Matthew — who Mark and Luke call Levi, son of Alphaeus — ran a tax booth there for Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee under Rome.
The system invited corruption.
Tax collectors paid for the right to collect, and anything they charged above the official amount was their profit.
Many got rich by overcharging their own neighbors, backed by soldiers.
Jewish religious teachers grouped them with robbers and prostitutes; their money was considered dirty, and devout people wouldn’t eat with them.
So Matthew was probably wealthy, educated enough to keep records, and almost completely shunned by respectable society.
Two words.
Jesus had been teaching and healing in Capernaum, often in Peter’s house a short walk away.
Not long before, Jesus had healed a paralyzed man lowered through the roof of a house there, and had shocked the religious leaders by telling him, “Your sins are forgiven.”
Matthew must have heard about it.
Then one day Jesus walked out along the lakeshore, past the tax booth, saw Matthew sitting there, and said, “Follow Me.”
Matthew got up and followed Him.
Luke adds that he “left everything.”
Fishermen like Peter could always return to their boats.
A tax collector who abandoned his post couldn’t walk back in and get the contract again.
Matthew’s decision was permanent, and costly.
Matthew’s own Gospel tells the story in just one verse, with no drama about himself — just the call and the response.
The party.
Matthew’s first act as a follower of Jesus was to throw a big banquet at his house in Jesus’ honor.
And he invited the only friends he had: other tax collectors and people religious society considered “sinners.”
A large crowd of them reclined at the table with Jesus and His disciples.
The Pharisees and their teachers were horrified.
Sharing a meal meant accepting someone.
They complained to Jesus’ disciples: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus answered them directly: “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.
I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
Matthew’s Gospel adds that Jesus told them to go and learn what the prophet Hosea meant: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”
The dinner showed what Matthew understood about Jesus right from the start: He had come for people like him — and his friends.
His Gospel.
The Gospel of Matthew doesn’t name its author, but the early church unanimously credited it to the apostle Matthew.
Around AD 120, a bishop named Papias wrote that Matthew compiled the sayings of Jesus in the Hebrew language.
The Gospel is written especially for Jewish readers.
It opens with Jesus’ family tree going back to Abraham and David, and it repeatedly says, “This took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet.”
It contains more than 60 Old Testament quotations.
It also gathers Jesus’ teaching into five big speeches, including the Sermon on the Mount, with the Beatitudes and the Lord’s Prayer.

Fittingly for a former tax collector, Matthew’s Gospel contains several stories about money and taxes, including one only he records: Jesus telling Peter to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth to pay the Temple tax.
Matthew’s Gospel ends with the Great Commission: “Go and make disciples of all nations… And surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”
How it ended.
Matthew is last named in the Bible among the apostles praying in Jerusalem after Jesus ascended, before the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost.
The Bible doesn’t say where he went after that.
Eusebius wrote that Matthew first preached to the Jews in Judea before going to other nations.
Different traditions have said he ministered in Ethiopia, in Persia, or among the Parthians, and most have said he died as a martyr, though the accounts don’t agree on how or where.
Matthew’s feast day is September 21 in the Western church.
In art he is often shown with an angel or a winged man — the symbol of his Gospel, which begins with Jesus’ human family tree — and sometimes with a money bag, remembering where Jesus found him.
Why Matthew matters today.
Matthew’s Gospel ends with Jesus’ command to “go and make disciples of all nations” and the promise, “I am with you always.”
The man who once collected money from people spent the rest of his life giving them something far more valuable.
Who he was.
James son of Alphaeus is one of the least-known apostles.
He is listed in all four lists of the twelve but never quoted or described.
He is often identified with “James the younger” (or “James the Less”), whose mother Mary stood watching at the crucifixion.
Since Matthew (Levi) is also called “son of Alphaeus,” some have wondered whether they were brothers, but the Bible never says so.
The Bible doesn’t say how he met Jesus or why Jesus chose him.
What we know is that he was there through everything — and that Jesus chose him by name, after praying all night.
Chosen.
Luke says Jesus spent the night on a mountain praying before choosing the twelve.
This James is always ninth in the lists, called “son of Alphaeus” to distinguish him from James son of Zebedee.
James the Less.
Mark names a woman at the cross as “Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses.”
Many identify this James with the son of Alphaeus.
“The Less” likely meant younger or smaller in stature — not less important.
There for everything.
He was among the twelve sent out to heal and preach, at the Last Supper, in the upper room after the resurrection, and praying when the Holy Spirit came.
The Bible doesn’t say how he died, and traditions have said different things.
Why he matters today.
Most of Jesus’ followers throughout history have been like James son of Alphaeus: faithful, present, and unknown.
His place among the twelve is a reminder that being chosen and loved by Jesus doesn’t depend on being famous.
Who he was.
This apostle goes by different names in different Gospels.
Matthew and Mark call him Thaddaeus (in some manuscripts, Lebbaeus); Luke and Acts call him Judas son of James.
John refers to him as “Judas (not Judas Iscariot)” to avoid confusion with the betrayer.
Most English speakers know him as Jude.
He should not be confused with Jude, the brother of Jesus, who wrote the letter of Jude, though some traditions have combined the two.
The Bible doesn’t say how he met Jesus or why Jesus chose him.
He speaks only once in the Gospels — and it’s a good question.
Many names.
After the betrayal, the name Judas carried a stain, which may be why some writers preferred Thaddaeus.
He should not be confused with Jude the brother of Jesus, who wrote the short letter of Jude (though some traditions combine them).
His question.
Jesus had said He would reveal Himself to those who love Him.
Jude, perhaps expecting a public, kingly Messiah, asked why not to everyone.
Jesus answered, “Anyone who loves Me will obey My teaching.
My Father will love them, and We will come to them and make Our home with them.”
How it ended.
Western tradition honors Jude and Simon together on October 28.
Jude became known as the patron saint of desperate cases and lost causes — possibly because people avoided praying to someone named Judas, so he was the saint of last resort.
Why he matters today.
Jude’s question — why Jesus reveals Himself to some and not to the whole world — is one many people still ask.
Jesus’ answer is that He makes His home with anyone who loves Him and keeps His word.
Who he was.
Simon is always identified as “the Zealot” (Luke) or “the Cananean” (Matthew and Mark, from an Aramaic word meaning “zealous”).
The title separates him from Simon Peter.
In first-century Judea, “zealots” were Jews passionate for God’s law and Israel’s freedom; some favored violent resistance to Roman occupation.
A few decades after Jesus, the Zealot movement led the Jewish revolt that ended with Rome destroying Jerusalem in AD 70.
The Bible doesn’t say how Simon met Jesus or why Jesus chose him.
But the label tells us he came to Jesus with strong political convictions — and ended up sharing meals every day with Matthew, a man who had worked for the very system he hated.
The Zealot.
Some Zealots later led a violent revolt against Rome (AD 66–70).
Whether Simon belonged to that movement or was simply known for his zeal, the label suggests a man who wanted God’s kingdom to come by force.
An unlikely team.
In ordinary life these two might have been enemies.
In Jesus’ company, they were brothers who ate, walked, prayed and preached together for three years.
How it ended.
Other traditions have placed him in Egypt or even Britain.
He is commemorated with Jude on October 28.
Why he matters today.
Jesus’ kingdom didn’t come the way Simon may have expected — not with swords, but with a cross.
Simon’s presence among the twelve shows that following Jesus can unite people across the deepest political divides.
Who Judas was.
Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles.
“Iscariot” most likely means “man of Kerioth,” a town in southern Judea, which would make him the only one of the twelve not from Galilee.
His father was named Simon.
Every list of the apostles places him last and adds a note: “who betrayed Him.”
Judas was not an outsider who slipped in.
He was chosen by Jesus after a night of prayer, sent out with the others to preach and heal, and trusted to keep the group’s money bag.
Why Jesus chose Judas.
This is one of the hardest questions in the Bible, and the Bible doesn’t say exactly why.
John’s Gospel says Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray Him, and Jesus once said, “Have I not chosen you, the Twelve?
Yet one of you is a devil.”
Jesus fulfilled the Scriptures, including a psalm about a close friend who shared bread and then turned against Him.
Yet Jesus treated Judas as a friend to the very end: He washed his feet, shared bread with him at the Last Supper, and even greeted him in the garden by calling him “friend.”
Judas was given every opportunity.
Chosen too.
Judas son of Simon Iscariot was chosen by Jesus as one of the twelve apostles after Jesus prayed all night on a mountain.
He traveled with Jesus for about three years.
He saw the blind receive sight and the dead raised, heard the Sermon on the Mount, and watched Jesus feed thousands.
When Jesus sent the twelve out two by two to preach that the kingdom of heaven was near, heal the sick and drive out demons, Judas was among them.
Nothing in the Gospels suggests the other disciples suspected him of anything.
In fact, the group trusted him enough to make him the treasurer, keeping the common money bag used for their needs and for giving to the poor.
A thief.
Six days before Passover, Jesus was at a dinner in Bethany with Lazarus, Martha and Mary.
Mary took a pint of pure nard, an expensive perfume imported from India, poured it on Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair.
The whole house filled with the fragrance.
Judas objected loudly: “Why wasn’t this perfume sold and the money given to the poor?
It was worth a year’s wages.” It sounded generous.
But John, who knew him well, explains: “He did not say this because he cared about the poor but because he was a thief; as keeper of the money bag, he used to help himself to what was put into it.”
Jesus defended Mary: “Leave her alone.
It was intended that she should save this perfume for the day of My burial.”
Matthew and Mark place Judas’s visit to the chief priests right after this dinner.
The deal.

The chief priests and elders had already gathered at the palace of Caiaphas, the high priest, and agreed to arrest Jesus secretly and kill Him — but not during the festival, because they feared a riot among the crowds who loved Him.
Judas solved their problem.
He went to them and asked, “What are you willing to give me if I deliver Him over to you?”
They counted out 30 pieces of silver.
Under the law of Moses, that was the payment for a slave who was killed, and the prophet Zechariah had described being valued at that same insulting price.
Luke and John both say that Satan entered Judas.
From then on, Judas watched for an opportunity to hand Jesus over when no crowd was present.
The kiss.
At the Last Supper, Jesus washed all the disciples’ feet, including Judas’s.
Then He said, deeply troubled, “One of you is going to betray Me.”
The disciples were stunned and asked, “Surely you don’t mean me, Lord?”
Jesus said it was the one to whom He would give a piece of bread dipped in the dish, and He handed it to Judas.
In that culture, offering someone a choice morsel was a gesture of honor and friendship.
Jesus told him, “What you are about to do, do quickly.” Judas went out.
John adds: “And it was night.”
Hours later, Judas led a large crowd with swords, clubs, torches and lanterns into the garden of Gethsemane — a place he knew because Jesus often met there with His disciples.
He had given them a signal: “The one I kiss is the man; arrest Him.”
A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.
Judas walked up, said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him.
Jesus answered, “Do what you came for, friend,” and in Luke, “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?”
Then the soldiers seized Him.
How it ended.
Early Friday morning, the council decided to hand Jesus over to Pilate to be executed.
When Judas saw that Jesus was condemned, Matthew says he was seized with remorse.
He brought the 30 pieces of silver back to the chief priests and elders and said, “I have sinned, for I have betrayed innocent blood.”
They answered coldly, “What is that to us?
That’s your responsibility.”
Judas threw the money into the Temple and went away and hanged himself.
The priests picked up the coins but said it was against the law to put blood money into the Temple treasury.
So they used it to buy a potter’s field as a burial place for foreigners, which became known as the Field of Blood.
Acts adds more details about how his body was found in that field.
Peter later said that Judas “was one of our number and shared in our ministry,” and the apostles chose Matthias to take his place.
Why Judas matters today.
Judas is a warning that it’s possible to be very close to Jesus — to see the miracles and hear the teaching — without truly following Him.
But his story also sits beside Peter’s.
Both failed Jesus on the same night.
The difference was what they did next: Peter came back to Jesus and was restored; Judas, filled with remorse, turned away in despair.
No failure is beyond Jesus’ forgiveness for anyone who returns to Him.
Who Matthias was.
Matthias was not one of the original twelve, but he was a long-time follower of Jesus.
Peter said the person replacing Judas needed to have been with them the whole time — from John’s baptism until Jesus was taken up to heaven — and to be a witness of the resurrection.
