That means Matthias had quietly followed Jesus for about three years without being named an apostle.
Some have suggested he was one of the 72 disciples Jesus sent out to preach, though the Bible doesn’t say.
After his selection, the Bible never mentions him again.
A faithful follower.
Peter set the requirement: the replacement must have been with them the whole time Jesus went in and out among them, and be a witness of the resurrection.
That means there were followers beyond the twelve who had been there from the start.
Chosen.
They prayed, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart.
Show us which of these two You have chosen.”
Casting lots was an Old Testament way of seeking God’s decision.
This is the last time it’s used in the Bible — soon after, the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost.
The Bible doesn’t say what he did next, but tradition has said Matthias preached in Judea and beyond and was martyred.
Why he matters today.
Matthias was faithful long before he had a title.
When the moment came, he was ready.
His story honors everyone who follows Jesus faithfully in the background.
Who Jesus is.
Jesus of Nazareth is the center of the whole Bible.
He is the eternal Son of God, the second person of the Trinity — Father, Son and Holy Spirit — who existed before creation and through whom all things were made.
About 2,000 years ago, He became a human being, born as a baby in Bethlehem.
He did not stop being God; He added a full human nature.
That’s why the Bible calls Him both “Son of God” and “Son of Man.”
He lived about 33 years in Roman-occupied Israel.
He spent most of them in Nazareth, a small village in Galilee, working as a craftsman like His legal father Joseph.

Around age 30 He began a public ministry of teaching, healing and calling disciples that lasted about three years, ending with His death by crucifixion in Jerusalem under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, His resurrection three days later, and His ascension into heaven.

Besides the four Gospels, Jesus is mentioned by ancient non-Christian writers, including the Jewish historian Josephus and the Roman historian Tacitus, who records that “Christus” was executed by Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius.
What the Old Testament promised.
For centuries before Jesus was born, the prophets described someone God would send.

He would be a descendant of Abraham through whom all nations would be blessed, a son of King David whose kingdom would last forever, a prophet like Moses, born in Bethlehem, coming to Jerusalem riding on a donkey, suffering and being “pierced for our transgressions,” and not being abandoned to the grave.
Jesus told His disciples after His resurrection that everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled.
The Word became flesh.
John’s Gospel opens: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God… The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.”
He is fully God and fully man — not half of each.
He was born a real baby, grew up, got hungry and tired, wept, and died a real death.
His name, Yeshua in Hebrew, means “the Lord saves.”
“Christ” is not a last name but a title — the Greek for Messiah, “the anointed one,” the King God had promised for centuries.
Born in Bethlehem.

A Roman census forced Joseph and Mary to travel about 90 miles from Nazareth to Bethlehem, Joseph’s ancestral town — fulfilling the prophet Micah, who said the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem.
There was no space in the guest room, so the newborn was laid in a feeding trough.
That night an angel appeared to shepherds outside town: “Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you; He is the Messiah, the Lord.”
A crowd of angels filled the sky praising God.
The shepherds hurried to find the baby and spread the news.
Wise men and a wicked king.
Magi — scholars who studied the stars — arrived in Jerusalem asking where the newborn King of the Jews was.
King Herod, paranoid about rivals, pretended he wanted to worship too.
The star led the Magi to the house in Bethlehem, where they gave gold, frankincense and myrrh.
Warned in a dream, they went home another way.
An angel warned Joseph to flee to Egypt.
Herod then ordered every boy two years old and under in Bethlehem killed.
After Herod died, the family returned and settled in Nazareth.
Twelve years old in the Temple.
It’s the only story we have of Jesus’ childhood.
His family traveled in a big group of relatives for Passover, so Mary and Joseph went a whole day before realizing He wasn’t with them.
After three days of searching they found Him sitting with the teachers, listening and asking questions.
Mary said, “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.”
He answered, “Didn’t you know I had to be in My Father’s house?”
Then He went home and obeyed them, and grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and people.
He worked as a carpenter until about age 30.
Baptized and tested.
As He came up out of the Jordan, the Spirit came down like a dove and the Father’s voice spoke — Father, Son and Spirit all present.
Then the Spirit led Him into the desert.
After 40 days without food, Satan tempted Him three times: turn stones into bread, jump from the Temple to prove God would catch Him, and bow down to get all the kingdoms of the world.
Each time Jesus answered with Scripture: “Man shall not live on bread alone,”
“Do not put the Lord your God to the test,”
“Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.”
Where Adam failed in a garden, Jesus held firm in a wilderness.
Water into wine.
When the wine ran out, Mary told Jesus, then told the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.”
He had them fill six stone jars used for ritual washing — each holding 20 to 30 gallons — with water.
When the master of the banquet tasted it, it was wine, and better than what had been served first.
John calls it the first of His signs, revealing His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.
Calling the twelve.
He called Peter, Andrew, James and John from their boats and Matthew from his tax booth.
He chose twelve — matching the twelve tribes of Israel — to be with Him, to preach and to drive out demons.
They were mostly ordinary, uneducated working men.
He trained them for about three years by living with them.
The Sermon on the Mount.
“Blessed are the poor in spirit… blessed are those who mourn… blessed are the meek… blessed are the peacemakers.”
He taught that anger is like murder in the heart and lust is like adultery.
Instead of revenge: turn the other cheek.
Pray for those who persecute you.
Don’t worry about tomorrow — look at the birds; your Father feeds them.
Do to others what you want them to do to you.
He ended with the wise man who built his house on the rock.
The crowds were amazed, because He taught as one with authority.
Healing the hurting.
He touched a man with leprosy — something no one did — and he was clean.
Four friends lowered a paralyzed man through a roof, and Jesus first said, “Your sins are forgiven,” then told him to walk.
A woman bleeding for twelve years touched His cloak and was healed.
He opened blind eyes and deaf ears.
He raised Jairus’s daughter, a widow’s only son at Nain, and His friend Lazarus after four days in the tomb.
The miracles showed His power and His compassion — and pointed to who He is.
Lord of the storm.
Jesus was asleep on a cushion in the back of the boat while it filled with water.
The terrified disciples woke Him: “Teacher, don’t You care if we drown?”
He got up, rebuked the wind and the sea, and there was a dead calm.
Then He asked, “Why are you so afraid?
Do you still have no faith?”
They were more terrified than before: “Who is this?
Even the wind and the waves obey Him!”
On another night He walked across the lake to them.
Feeding the 5,000.
The count was 5,000 men, besides women and children.
He had them sit on the green grass in groups, gave thanks, broke the bread and kept giving it to the disciples to hand out.
The next day He told the crowd, “I am the bread of life.
Whoever comes to Me will never go hungry.”
Many followers found that teaching too hard and left.
Jesus asked the twelve, “Do you want to leave too?”
Peter answered, “Lord, to whom would we go?
You have the words of eternal life.”
Stories that stick.
A parable is a short, everyday story with a deeper point.
When a lawyer asked “Who is my neighbor?”, Jesus told about a Samaritan — a despised outsider — who stopped to help a beaten man that religious leaders walked past.
He told about a shepherd who leaves 99 sheep to find one, and a father who runs to welcome home a son who wasted everything.
The kingdom of God, He said, is like a tiny mustard seed that grows into a tree, or like treasure hidden in a field worth selling everything for.
Friend of sinners.
He went to Zacchaeus’s house, let a sinful woman wash His feet with her tears, and said to a woman dragged before Him for adultery, “Neither do I condemn you. Go and sin no more.”
When disciples shooed children away, He said, “Let the little children come to Me.”
His critics called Him “a friend of tax collectors and sinners.”
He said, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
Who do you say I am?.
Jesus made claims no ordinary teacher would make: “I am the light of the world,”
“I am the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep,”
“I am the resurrection and the life,”
“Before Abraham was, I am” — using God’s own name.
He forgave sins, which only God can do.
Three times He predicted His death and resurrection.
The disciples didn’t understand.
Palm Sunday.
The prophet Zechariah had said Israel’s king would come “humble and riding on a donkey.”
Crowds spread cloaks and branches on the road.
Days later He overturned the tables of merchants and money changers in the Temple courts: “My house will be called a house of prayer, but you are making it a den of robbers.”
The chief priests began looking for a way to kill Him, but were afraid of the crowds.
The Last Supper.
He took bread: “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”
He took the cup: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, poured out for you.”
He gave them a new command: “Love one another as I have loved you.”
He promised to send the Holy Spirit and prayed for them and for all who would believe through them.
Gethsemane.
He was so distressed His sweat was like drops of blood.
Three times He found the disciples sleeping.
Judas identified Him with a kiss.
Peter swung a sword; Jesus healed the wounded servant and let Himself be arrested. All the disciples fled.
On trial.
False witnesses contradicted each other.
The high priest finally asked, “Are You the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One?”
Jesus said, “I am,” and they condemned Him for blasphemy.
Since only Rome could execute, they took Him to Pilate, accusing Him of claiming to be a king.
Pilate said, “I find no basis for a charge.”
The crowd demanded the release of Barabbas, a murderer, instead, and shouted, “Crucify Him!”
Pilate had Jesus flogged, soldiers crowned Him with thorns, and Pilate handed Him over.
The cross.
Around nine in the morning they nailed Him to a cross on Golgotha.
Above Him was a sign: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.”
He prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
He promised a dying thief, “Today you will be with Me in paradise.”
Darkness covered the land from noon until three.
He cried, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” then, “It is finished,” and “Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit.”
The Temple curtain tore from top to bottom.
Isaiah had written: “He was pierced for our transgressions… by His wounds we are healed.”
He is risen.
Women came at dawn with spices and found the stone rolled away.
Angels said, “Why do you look for the living among the dead?
He is not here; He has risen!”
He appeared to Mary Magdalene in the garden, to two disciples walking to Emmaus, to the apostles behind locked doors, to Thomas, and to seven of them by the lake.
He ate with them and showed them His wounds.
Paul, writing about 25 years later, lists the witnesses — including over 500 at once, most of them still alive to be asked.
Ascended — and coming back.
“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.
Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit… and surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age.”
Then He was taken up before their eyes, and two angels said, “This same Jesus will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven.”
Ten days later the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost, and the church began.
Why Jesus came.
Jesus said, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost,” and “to give His life as a ransom for many.”

The Bible teaches that every person has sinned and is separated from God, and that Jesus, who never sinned, died in our place and rose again so that anyone who trusts in Him is forgiven and receives eternal life.
“For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that whoever believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.”
Why Jesus matters today.
Jesus is not only a figure from history.
He is risen and alive, and He promised to return.
He invites everyone, as He invited Peter and Matthew: “Follow Me.”
He also said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.”
Who Mary was.
Mary (Miriam in Hebrew) was a young Jewish woman from Nazareth, a small farming village in Galilee.
She was probably in her early-to-mid teens when the Bible story begins, the normal age for engagement then.
She was engaged to Joseph, a craftsman descended from King David, and she was related to Elizabeth, the wife of a priest named Zechariah.
Nothing in her background made her famous.
Nazareth was so insignificant it isn’t mentioned once in the Old Testament.
God chose an ordinary young woman in an ordinary village to be the mother of His Son.
Why God chose Mary.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why God chose Mary, but the angel Gabriel called her “highly favored” and said “the Lord is with you.”

Her response shows her character: she asked an honest question (“How will this be?”), then fully trusted God even though saying yes could cost her her engagement, her reputation and possibly her life.
Her song of praise, the Magnificat, shows she knew the Scriptures deeply.
Engaged in Nazareth.
Jewish engagement was a legally binding commitment — breaking it required a divorce — but the couple didn’t live together yet.
Mary was a relative of Elizabeth, the wife of a priest.
Her name in Hebrew is Miriam, after Moses’ sister.
The angel Gabriel.
Gabriel greeted her: “Rejoice, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.” She was troubled.
He said she would have a son named Jesus who would reign on David’s throne forever.
She asked, “How will this be, since I am a virgin?”
He said the Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her.
“Nothing is impossible with God.”
Mary answered, “May it be to me according to your word.”
She knew an unexplained pregnancy could cost her her engagement, her reputation, even her life.
Visiting Elizabeth.
Elizabeth, pregnant with John the Baptist in her old age, was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!”
Mary’s song begins, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior.”
It praises God who lifts up the humble and fills the hungry.
She stayed about three months.
The birth.
Forty days later, at the Temple, an old man named Simeon took the baby in his arms and praised God, then told Mary: “A sword will pierce your own soul too.”
Then came the Magi, the escape to Egypt, and the return to Nazareth.
“Do whatever He tells you”.
Those are her last recorded words in John’s Gospel — and good advice for anyone.
Jesus turned the water into wine.
Mary also appears during His ministry, once coming with His brothers to take Him home because people said He was out of His mind.
At the cross.
Simeon’s prophecy of a sword piercing her soul came true.
Even in agony, Jesus made sure she would be cared for, and John took her into his home.
With the church.
Acts names “Mary the mother of Jesus” among those praying constantly in the upper room — the last time the Bible mentions her.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians honor her as the Mother of God (Theotokos), since the child she bore is God the Son.
Why Mary matters today.
Mary is the only person present at both Jesus’ birth and His death, and she was with the church at its beginning.
Her life models faith and obedience: “I am the Lord’s servant.
May it be to me according to your word.”
And her last recorded words in the Gospels are still the best advice: “Do whatever He tells you.”
Who Joseph was.
Joseph was a craftsman (tekton) in Nazareth — someone who worked with wood or stone, building furniture, tools or houses.
He was a descendant of King David and engaged to Mary.
Matthew calls him “a righteous man.”
He became the legal father of Jesus, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and raised Him as his own son, giving Him His name, His trade, and His legal place in David’s royal line.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why God chose Joseph, but it shows a man of quiet integrity who protected others and obeyed God immediately, every single time.
A righteous man.
The Greek word for his trade, tekton, means a builder or craftsman working in wood or stone.
Matthew’s Gospel traces his family line back through King David to Abraham, which is how Jesus legally became “Son of David.”
The dream.
Joseph was “a righteous man and did not want to expose her to public disgrace,” so he planned a quiet divorce.
Then an angel said, “Do not be afraid to take Mary home as your wife… She will give birth to a son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins.”
When Joseph woke up, he did exactly what the angel said.
Protector.
Joseph received four dreams in Matthew’s Gospel and obeyed every one immediately: marry Mary, flee to Egypt, return to Israel, and settle in Galilee instead of Judea.
He named Jesus, presented Him at the Temple, and taught Him his trade.
Searching for Jesus.
This is the last time Joseph appears alive in the Gospels.
He was likely dead before Jesus’ ministry began, since he isn’t mentioned at the cross, where Jesus entrusted Mary to John.
Joseph never speaks a single recorded word in the Bible.
Why Joseph matters today.
Joseph never speaks a single word in the Bible, yet he protected the Son of God and His mother through scandal, exile and danger.
He shows that faithful, quiet obedience can shape history.
Who John was.
John was born about six months before Jesus to an elderly priest, Zechariah, and his wife Elizabeth, a relative of Mary.
His birth was announced by the angel Gabriel, who said he would be filled with the Holy Spirit even before he was born and would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah.”
When pregnant Mary visited Elizabeth, the baby John leaped in Elizabeth’s womb.
As an adult, John lived in the Judean wilderness and became the most famous prophet in Israel in centuries.
Even the Jewish historian Josephus wrote about him.
His job, foretold by Isaiah and Malachi, was to prepare people for the Messiah.
How John knew Jesus.
John and Jesus were relatives, though John said he did not fully recognize who Jesus was until God showed him a sign: the Spirit descending like a dove at Jesus’ baptism.
From then on, John pointed his own followers to Jesus: “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
Several of Jesus’ first disciples, including Andrew, came from John’s circle.
A miracle baby.
Zechariah was serving in the Temple when Gabriel appeared and said the boy would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah.”
Because Zechariah asked for proof, he couldn’t speak for nine months.
When relatives wanted to name the baby after his father, Zechariah wrote on a tablet, “His name is John,” and his voice came back.
The voice in the desert.
Crowds came out from Jerusalem and all Judea.
He told soldiers not to extort money, tax collectors not to overcharge, and anyone with two coats to share.
He called the religious leaders a “brood of vipers.”
Isaiah had foretold him: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord.’”
“Behold, the Lamb of God”.
At first John tried to stop Jesus: “I need to be baptized by You!”
When some of John’s followers worried that everyone was going to Jesus now, John said, “He must become greater; I must become less.”
Doubts in prison.
Jesus answered by pointing to what was happening: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news.
Then He told the crowd that no one born of a woman was greater than John.
How it ended.
Herodias’s daughter danced for Herod and his guests, and he promised her anything.
Prompted by her mother, she asked for John’s head on a platter.
Herod was distressed but didn’t want to break his oath in front of guests.
The Jewish historian Josephus also records John’s execution by Herod.
Why John matters today.
Jesus said that among those born of women there was no one greater than John.
His greatness came from his humility: “He must become greater; I must become less.”
His life was entirely about pointing people to Jesus.
Who Mary Magdalene was.
Mary Magdalene came from Magdala, a prosperous fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, known for salting and exporting fish.
“Magdalene” simply means “from Magdala.”
Jesus freed her from seven demons, and from then on she became one of His most devoted followers, traveling with Him and the twelve and helping to fund His ministry with her own money.
She is often confused with the unnamed sinful woman who anointed Jesus’ feet, or with Mary of Bethany, but the Bible never connects them.
The idea that she had been a prostitute comes from a sermon by Pope Gregory in AD 591, not from Scripture.
Set free.
Luke names her first among several women Jesus had healed who traveled with Him and the twelve, supporting them out of their own money.
She is often confused with the sinful woman who anointed Jesus’ feet, but the Bible never says that was her.
She stayed.
All four Gospels place her at the crucifixion.
She saw Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lay the body in the tomb and roll the stone across, and went home to prepare spices for after the Sabbath.
The empty tomb.
She assumed someone had taken the body: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have put Him!”
Peter and John ran, looked, and went home.
Mary stayed outside, crying.
“Mary!”.
Two angels asked why she was crying.
She turned and saw a man she thought was the gardener: “Sir, if you have carried Him away, tell me where.” Jesus said, “Mary.”
She cried out, “Rabboni!” (Teacher).
He sent her to tell the disciples: “I am ascending to My Father and your Father.”
She went and announced, “I have seen the Lord!” — earning her the ancient title “apostle to the apostles.”
Why Mary Magdalene matters today.
In an age when women’s testimony wasn’t accepted in court, Jesus chose a woman to be the first witness of His resurrection and sent her to tell the apostles.
She was there when others ran — at the cross, at the tomb, and in the garden where she heard Him say her name.
Who they were.
Martha and Mary were sisters who lived with their brother Lazarus in Bethany, a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem.
Their home was where Jesus stayed during visits to Jerusalem, especially in His last week.
John’s Gospel says plainly: “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.”
Martha seems to have been the older sister and the host — practical, busy and outspoken.
Mary was more reflective, the one who sat at Jesus’ feet.
Both loved Him deeply and both made strong statements of faith.
An open home.
John says simply, “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.”
Their home was a place of rest for Him during visits to Jerusalem.
Busy vs. listening.
Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the posture of a disciple — unusual for a woman then.
Martha, overwhelmed, asked Jesus to tell Mary to help.
He answered gently, “Martha, Martha, you are worried and upset about many things, but few things are needed — or indeed only one.
Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken from her.”
“If You had been here…”.
Martha went out to meet Jesus and said, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.
But I know that even now God will give You whatever You ask.”
Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life.
Whoever believes in Me will live, even though they die. Do you believe this?”
Martha answered, “Yes, Lord.
I believe that You are the Messiah, the Son of God.”
Mary came and fell at His feet weeping, and Jesus wept with her. Then He raised Lazarus.
The perfume.
The nard was worth about a year’s wages.
The house filled with the fragrance.
Judas complained; Jesus said, “Leave her alone.
She has kept this for the day of My burial.”
Martha, true to form, was serving the dinner.
Why they matter today.
Martha and Mary show that Jesus has real friendships with real people.
He gently corrected Martha’s anxiety, defended Mary’s devotion, wept with them in grief, and gave them one of His greatest promises: “I am the resurrection and the life.”
Who Lazarus was.
Lazarus lived in Bethany with his sisters Martha and Mary.
He was a close friend of Jesus — when he got sick, the message his sisters sent simply said, “Lord, the one You love is sick.”
His name is a form of Eleazar, meaning “God has helped.”
He is a different person from the poor man named Lazarus in Jesus’ parable of the rich man.
“The one You love is sick”.
Jesus said the sickness would not end in death but was for God’s glory.
Then He told the disciples, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him up.”
They thought He meant actual sleep, so He told them plainly, “Lazarus is dead.”
Jesus wept.
Jewish belief held that the soul lingered near the body for three days — four days meant hopelessly dead.
Jesus was deeply moved and troubled.
“Jesus wept” is the shortest verse in most English Bibles.
The onlookers said, “See how He loved him!”
“Lazarus, come out!”.
Martha warned, “By this time there is a bad odor.”
Jesus said, “Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?”
He thanked the Father aloud so the crowd would believe, then called in a loud voice.
Jesus said, “Take off the grave clothes and let him go.”
A marked man.
From that day the council planned Jesus’ death.
Crowds came to Bethany just to see Lazarus, so the chief priests made plans to kill him as well, because on account of him many were believing in Jesus.
A week later Lazarus was at the dinner where Mary anointed Jesus.
Why Lazarus matters today.
Raising Lazarus was the last and greatest of the miracles John records before the cross, and it directly led to the plot to kill Jesus.
It was a preview of Jesus’ own resurrection a week later — and of His promise: “Whoever believes in Me will live, even though they die.”
Who Nicodemus was.
Nicodemus was a Pharisee — a member of a strict, respected Jewish group devoted to keeping God’s law — and a member of the Sanhedrin, the 71-member ruling council in Jerusalem.
Jesus called him “Israel’s teacher,” so he was a well-known scholar.
He was likely wealthy, judging by the expensive burial spices he later brought.
How Nicodemus knew Jesus: he had seen or heard about Jesus’ miracles and came to Him at night to ask questions, saying, “We know You are a teacher who has come from God.”
A visit at night.
He was a member of the Sanhedrin, the 71-member Jewish ruling council, and Jesus called him “Israel’s teacher.”
Coming at night likely kept the visit hidden from his colleagues.
Born again.
Nicodemus took it literally: “How can someone be born when they are old?”
Jesus explained a birth of water and the Spirit.
Then: “For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that whoever believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.”
Speaking up.
The others mocked him: “Are you from Galilee too?”
It was a small, risky step into the open.
Burying Jesus.
That amount of spices was fit for a king’s burial.
With Joseph of Arimathea he wrapped the body in linen and laid it in a new tomb.
The man who came in the dark now stepped forward publicly — at the moment the disciples were hiding.
Why Nicodemus matters today.
Nicodemus’s faith grew slowly — from secret questions, to quietly defending Jesus in the council, to publicly burying Him when the disciples were hiding.
Jesus gave him, and the world, John 3:16.
Who Zacchaeus was.
Zacchaeus was the chief tax collector in Jericho, a wealthy city on a major trade route.
As a “chief” tax collector he oversaw others and profited from all their collections.
He was rich, short, and hated by his neighbors as a cheater and collaborator with Rome.
How Zacchaeus knew Jesus: he had obviously heard about Jesus — perhaps that He was a friend of tax collectors — and was so curious that he climbed a tree just to see Him pass by.
Rich and hated.
Jericho was a wealthy trade city on the road to Jerusalem.
As chief tax collector he oversaw other collectors and profited from all of them.
His name ironically means “pure” or “innocent.”
Up a tree.
Grown men of rank didn’t run or climb trees.
Zacchaeus didn’t care how it looked.
“Hurry down”.
Of all the people in Jericho, Jesus chose to be the guest of the most despised man there.
Zacchaeus came down at once and welcomed Him gladly.
Everyone muttered, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinner.”
A changed man.
The law only required repaying the amount plus a fifth.
Jesus said, “Today salvation has come to this house… For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
Why Zacchaeus matters today.
Jesus noticed the one person everyone else despised, called him by name, and invited Himself to his house.
Zacchaeus’s generous change of heart came after Jesus accepted him, not before.
Jesus summed it up: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”
Who Paul was.
Paul was born in Tarsus, a major city in what is now southern Turkey, around AD 5.
He was Jewish, from the tribe of Benjamin, and his parents named him Saul after Israel’s first king.
He was also born a Roman citizen, a valuable status that later saved his life more than once. Paul was his Roman name.
As a young man he moved to Jerusalem and studied under Gamaliel, one of the most respected rabbis of the day.
He became a Pharisee, and he says he was advancing beyond others his age in zeal for the traditions of his ancestors.
He also learned a trade, tentmaking, which he used to support himself throughout his ministry.
How Paul met Jesus.
Paul never met Jesus during His earthly ministry.
He was the church’s fiercest enemy: he approved Stephen’s execution and went from house to house dragging Christians to prison.
Then on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus appeared to him in a blinding light and spoke to him by name.
Paul later counted this as a true resurrection appearance — the last one — and it made him an apostle.
Why Jesus chose Paul.
Jesus told Ananias, the man sent to heal Paul’s blindness: “This man is My chosen instrument to proclaim My name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel.
I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.”
Paul himself said he was “the worst of sinners,” and that God showed him mercy so that he could be an example of Christ’s patience to everyone who would believe.
Saul of Tarsus.
He described himself as “a Hebrew of Hebrews… as for zeal, persecuting the church; as for righteousness based on the law, faultless.”
He made tents for a living.
Saul was his Hebrew name; Paul was his Roman one.
Hunting Christians.
He held the coats of the men who stoned Stephen.
Then he got letters from the high priest to arrest followers of “the Way” in Damascus and bring them back to Jerusalem in chains.
The Damascus road.
Saul was blind for three days and didn’t eat or drink.
God sent a disciple named Ananias — terrified, because of Saul’s reputation — to lay hands on him.
Something like scales fell from his eyes, he was baptized, and immediately began preaching in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.
His former allies plotted to kill him, and he escaped Damascus lowered in a basket through a window in the city wall.
Barnabas vouches for him.
Paul spent years in Arabia, Damascus and his hometown of Tarsus.
Later Barnabas went to find him and brought him to Antioch, where the believers were first called Christians.
Missionary journeys.
He usually started in the local synagogue, then reached Gentiles.
In Lystra he was stoned and left for dead, then got up and went back into the city.
In Athens he preached on Mars Hill about “the unknown god.”
In Ephesus a riot broke out because the silversmiths who made idols were losing business.
He worked making tents so he wouldn’t be a burden.
Singing in prison.
They had freed a slave girl from a spirit that let her owners make money telling fortunes.
The jailer woke, saw the doors open, and was about to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had escaped.
Paul shouted, “Don’t harm yourself! We are all here!”
The jailer asked, “What must I do to be saved?”
“Believe in the Lord Jesus.”
He and his whole household were baptized that night.
What he suffered.
He lists it himself: “in danger from rivers, bandits, my own people, Gentiles… I have known hunger and thirst… I have been cold and naked.”
He also had a “thorn in the flesh”
God didn’t remove, and heard God say, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is made perfect in weakness.”
His letters.
Romans explains salvation by grace through faith. 1 Corinthians 13 says, “Love is patient, love is kind.”
Philippians, written from prison, says, “Rejoice in the Lord always,” and “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.”
Galatians says, “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”
Arrested and shipwrecked.
A mob in the Temple nearly killed him.
He spent two years in custody in Caesarea, testifying before governors and King Agrippa.
As a Roman citizen he appealed to the emperor.
On the voyage a storm raged for two weeks; Paul told all 276 on board that an angel promised no one would die.
The ship broke apart off Malta, and everyone made it to shore.
A snake bit him and he was unharmed.
How it ended.
Acts ends with Paul in Rome “proclaiming the kingdom of God… with all boldness and without hindrance.”
His last letter, to Timothy, says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”
Clement of Rome and later writers record his martyrdom in Rome around AD 64–67.
As a citizen he would have been beheaded rather than crucified.
What made Paul extraordinary.

Paul traveled roughly 10,000 miles on foot and by ship, planted churches across modern-day Turkey and Greece, wrote 13 of the 27 books of the New Testament, and preached to synagogues, philosophers, governors and kings.
More than anyone, he carried the message of Jesus from a Jewish movement in Judea to the wider Roman world.
Why Paul matters today.
Paul’s life is the clearest example of God’s grace: the man who hunted Christians became the greatest missionary.
His letters still shape how Christians understand salvation, love and the church.
Near the end he wrote, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.”
Who Stephen was.
Stephen was one of the early believers in Jerusalem, likely a Greek-speaking Jew.
When the apostles needed help distributing food fairly to widows, the church chose seven men “full of the Spirit and wisdom,” and Stephen was the first named.
He did far more than serve tables: he performed great wonders and signs and debated so powerfully that his opponents couldn’t answer him.
The Bible doesn’t say whether Stephen ever met Jesus in person.
What it shows is that he knew the Scriptures deeply and was filled with the Holy Spirit.
Chosen to serve.
The requirement was men “full of the Spirit and wisdom.”
Stephen is described as “full of faith and of the Holy Spirit” and “full of God’s grace and power,” performing great wonders and signs.
Falsely accused.
He was dragged before the Sanhedrin.
As they stared at him, they saw his face was like the face of an angel.
His great speech.
It’s the longest speech in Acts.
He ended: “You stiff-necked people!
You always resist the Holy Spirit… You have received the law but have not obeyed it.” The council was furious.
How it ended.
He cried, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” then knelt and said, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.”
A young man named Saul stood guarding the coats.
Stephen’s death triggered a persecution that scattered believers — who spread the message everywhere they went.
Why Stephen matters today.
Stephen was the first person to die for following Jesus.
He died the way Jesus did — praying for his killers.
His death scattered the church and spread the message far beyond Jerusalem, and the young man watching, Saul, would become the apostle Paul.
Who Barnabas was.
Barnabas was a Levite — from Israel’s priestly tribe — from the island of Cyprus.
His given name was Joseph, but the apostles nicknamed him Barnabas, “son of encouragement,” and the name stuck.
He was a cousin of John Mark.
He was generous, trusted, and willing to take risks on people others had written off.
The encourager.
He laid the money at the apostles’ feet to help believers in need.
Acts calls him “a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith.”
Taking a chance on Paul.
Later, when the church in Antioch was growing, Barnabas went to Tarsus to find Paul and brought him to help.
They taught there for a year.
The first missionary journey.
After Paul healed a lame man, the people shouted that the gods had come down — calling Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes — and tried to offer sacrifices.
The two tore their clothes and begged them to turn to the living God.
A second chance for Mark.
Mark had quit the first trip.
Barnabas, his cousin, wouldn’t give up on him.
Years later Paul wrote, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is helpful to me.”
Mark wrote the Gospel of Mark.
Why Barnabas matters today.
Without Barnabas, the church might never have trusted Paul, and Mark might never have written his Gospel.
Encouragers change history.
Who Timothy was.
Timothy came from Lystra in what is now Turkey.
His mother Eunice was a Jewish believer and his father was Greek.
He learned the Scriptures from his mother and grandmother Lois, and likely came to faith during Paul’s first visit to Lystra.
By Paul’s second visit, the believers spoke highly of him, and Paul invited him to join his team.
Sincere faith.
His father was Greek.
Paul wrote, “I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice.”
Joining Paul.
Paul called him “my true son in the faith” and sent him to strengthen churches in Thessalonica, Corinth and Philippi.
Six of Paul’s letters name Timothy as co-sender.
Letters to a young pastor.
Paul told him to set an example in speech, life, love, faith and purity, and that “God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love and self-discipline.”
Paul’s last letter, written from prison near his death, begs Timothy to come quickly.
Why Timothy matters today.
Timothy shows the power of faith passed down at home and of mentoring.
He was young and seems to have been timid, yet Paul trusted him with leading churches.
Who Lydia was.
Lydia came from Thyatira, a city in Asia Minor famous for its purple dye industry, and was living in Philippi in Macedonia selling expensive purple cloth.
She was a “worshiper of God” — a Gentile who believed in the God of Israel.
She was the head of her own household, suggesting she was a widow or single businesswoman of means.
A dealer in purple.
Purple dye was costly and associated with royalty, so her business served the wealthy.
Philippi didn’t have enough Jewish men for a synagogue, so worshipers met by the river.
Her heart opened.
She insisted Paul and his companions stay at her home.
After Paul and Silas were freed from prison, they went to Lydia’s house, where the believers met.
Her home became the first church in Philippi.
Why Lydia matters today.
Lydia was the first recorded convert in Europe, and her home became the first church in Philippi — the church Paul later wrote his warmest letter to.
Who they were.
Aquila was a Jew from Pontus, near the Black Sea; Priscilla (also called Prisca) was his wife.
They had lived in Rome until Emperor Claudius expelled the Jews around AD 49, then moved to Corinth, where they ran a tentmaking business.
Paul, a tentmaker too, stayed and worked with them.
They later moved to Ephesus and back to Rome, hosting churches in their home wherever they went.
Refugees and tentmakers.
The Roman historian Suetonius records Claudius expelling Jews from Rome around AD 49.
Paul shared their trade and lived with them for 18 months.
Teaching a teacher.
They did it privately and graciously.
Apollos went on to be a powerful leader in Corinth.
Risking their necks.
Paul writes, “Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my co-workers in Christ Jesus.
They risked their lives for me… Greet also the church that meets at their house.”
Priscilla is usually named first — unusual then, and perhaps a sign of her leadership.
Why they matter today.
Priscilla and Aquila show a married couple serving God together through their work, their home and their hospitality — and teaching others with grace.
Who Adam & Eve were.
Adam and Eve were the first human beings, created by God and placed in the Garden of Eden.
Genesis describes God forming Adam from the dust and breathing life into him, then making Eve from Adam’s side as his partner — equal in worth and made for each other.
They were given the job of caring for the earth and ruling it on God’s behalf.
Genesis says both were made “in the image of God,” which is why every human life has dignity.
Made by God.
“Adam” is the Hebrew word for human, related to adamah, ground.
God placed him in Eden to work the garden and take care of it, and had him name the animals.
None was a fitting partner, so God put Adam into a deep sleep and formed a woman from his rib.
Adam said, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
Eve’s name means “living,” because she would be the mother of all the living.
They were naked and felt no shame.
One rule.
God said, “You are free to eat from any tree in the garden; but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will certainly die.”
Everything else was theirs, including the tree of life.
The serpent.
The serpent twisted God’s words, then contradicted them.
Eve saw the fruit was good for food, pleasing to the eye, and desirable for gaining wisdom.
Adam was with her, and he ate too.
Their eyes were opened; they realized they were naked and sewed fig leaves together.
Hiding from God.
God called, “Where are you?”
Adam said he was afraid because he was naked.
God asked if he had eaten from the tree.
Adam said, “The woman You put here with me — she gave me some.”
Eve said, “The serpent deceived me.”
God announced the consequences: pain in childbirth, struggle in work, and death — “for dust you are and to dust you will return.”
But to the serpent He promised that a descendant of the woman would crush its head — the first promise of a Savior.
Out of Eden.
They lost access to the tree of life.
Outside Eden they had sons — Cain, Abel and later Seth — and other sons and daughters.
The Bible says Adam lived 930 years.
Paul later calls Jesus “the last Adam,” who succeeded where the first failed.
Why they matter today.
Their story explains why the world is both beautiful and broken.
It also contains the first promise of rescue: a descendant of Eve would crush the serpent.
The New Testament calls Jesus the “last Adam,” who undid what Adam lost.
Who Cain & Abel were.
Cain and Abel were the first two sons of Adam and Eve, born outside Eden.
Cain, the firstborn, became a farmer; Abel kept flocks.
Their story is the first account of worship in the Bible — and the first murder.
Two brothers, two offerings.
Abel brought fat portions from the firstborn of his flock; Cain brought “some of the fruits.”
Hebrews says Abel offered by faith.
Cain became very angry and his face was downcast.
Sin at the door.
God asked why he was angry and told him that if he did what was right, he would be accepted.
It was a chance to turn around.
“Am I my brother’s keeper?”.
God said, “Your brother’s blood cries out to Me from the ground.”
Cain was sentenced to be a restless wanderer.
He protested that anyone would kill him, so God put a mark on him so no one would.
Cain settled east of Eden in the land of Nod and built a city.
Adam and Eve later had Seth, through whom Noah’s line came.
Why it matters today.
God warned Cain that sin was crouching at his door and that he could master it.
Cain’s story shows how jealousy left unchecked grows into something terrible — and that even then, God showed Cain mercy.
Hebrews remembers Abel as a man of faith.
Who Noah was.
Noah lived in the tenth generation from Adam, in a world the Bible describes as filled with violence and corruption.
His father Lamech named him Noah, which sounds like the Hebrew word for “comfort” or “rest.”
Genesis says he was righteous, blameless among the people of his time, and that he “walked faithfully with God.”
He had three sons — Shem, Ham and Japheth — and the Bible traces every nation on earth back to them.
Why God chose Noah.
Genesis says simply that “Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord.”
Hebrews says he built the ark “by faith,” taking God’s warning seriously about things not yet seen.
Noah obeyed God completely for decades, building a huge boat on dry land while the world around him carried on as usual.
A violent world.
God saw that every inclination of human hearts was only evil all the time, and it grieved Him.
“But Noah found favor in the eyes of the Lord.”
He had three sons: Shem, Ham and Japheth.
Build an ark.
The ark was 300 cubits long, 50 wide and 30 high — three decks, coated with pitch inside and out.
It likely took decades to build.
Noah did everything just as God commanded.
The flood.
Noah was 600 years old.
God Himself shut the door.
The springs of the deep burst open and the floodgates of heaven opened.
The waters flooded the earth for 150 days.
The dove.
The ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.
The second time the dove came back in the evening with a freshly plucked olive leaf.
A week later it didn’t come back at all.
Noah’s family had been in the ark over a year.
The rainbow.
God blessed Noah and his sons: “Be fruitful and increase in number and fill the earth.”
Every nation, Genesis says, descends from Noah’s three sons.
Later Noah planted a vineyard, got drunk, and his son Ham dishonored him — even heroes of faith were flawed. Noah lived 950 years.
Why Noah matters today.
Noah’s story shows both God’s justice against evil and His mercy in providing a way of rescue.
The rainbow still reminds us of God’s promise.
Peter later compared the ark to how God saves His people through Jesus.
Who Abraham was.
Abraham, first called Abram, was born around 2000 BC in Ur of the Chaldeans, a wealthy city in Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq).
His family worshiped other gods.
He married Sarai, and they had no children.
His father Terah moved the family to Haran in northern Mesopotamia, and it was there, at 75, that God called Abram to leave everything.
Why God chose Abraham.
The Bible doesn’t say exactly why God chose Abraham, but it emphasizes his response: he believed God and obeyed, leaving home without knowing where he was going.
God’s plan was bigger than one man — through Abraham’s family, “all peoples on earth will be blessed.”
That promise was fulfilled through Jesus, a descendant of Abraham.
Go.
God promised: “I will make you into a great nation… and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you.”
Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot and everything they owned to Canaan, without knowing where he was going.
Count the stars.
“Abram believed the Lord, and He credited it to him as righteousness.”
God made a covenant with him in a strange ceremony, passing between cut animals as a smoking firepot and blazing torch — God taking the oath on Himself.
Hagar and Ishmael.
Abram was 86.
Hagar began to despise Sarai, and Sarai mistreated her until she ran away.
An angel found her by a spring and sent her back with a promise for her son.
God later promised Ishmael would also become a great nation.
A new name.
God promised that Sarah herself would have a son within a year.
Abraham fell facedown laughing at the idea of a 100-year-old and a 90-year-old having a baby.
Pleading for Sodom.
“Will not the Judge of all the earth do right?” God agreed each time.
Ten righteous people could not be found, but God rescued Abraham’s nephew Lot before destroying the city.
Isaac is born.
Sarah said, “God has brought me laughter, and everyone who hears about this will laugh with me.” Isaac means “he laughs.”
The test.
Isaac asked, “Where is the lamb?”
Abraham answered, “God Himself will provide the lamb.”
He bound Isaac on the altar and raised the knife.
The angel called, “Do not lay a hand on the boy.”
Abraham named the place “The Lord Will Provide.”
Hebrews says Abraham reasoned that God could raise the dead.
Mount Moriah is where Solomon later built the Temple in Jerusalem.
His legacy.
He bought a cave at Machpelah in Hebron to bury Sarah — his only land in the promised country — and was buried there too.
The New Testament calls him the father of all who believe.
Why Abraham matters today.
Abraham is called the father of faith.
Paul says that anyone who trusts God the way Abraham did is his spiritual child.
His life shows faith that waits, stumbles, grows, and finally trusts God even with what it loves most.
Who Sarah was.
Sarah, first called Sarai, was Abraham’s wife and half-sister.
She was famously beautiful.
For most of her life she couldn’t have children — a deep source of pain and shame in her culture.
She left her home and family to follow God’s call with Abraham at age 65.
Beautiful and barren.
In Egypt and later in Gerar, kings took her into their households until God intervened.
She was also Abram’s half-sister, so it was a half-truth.
Taking control.
It was a legal custom of the time, but it brought pain to everyone involved.
She laughed.
Afraid, she denied it: “I did not laugh.”
The Lord said, “Yes, you did.”
Laughter.
She died at 127 in Hebron, the only woman whose age at death is recorded in the Bible.
Hebrews lists her among the heroes of faith.
Why Sarah matters today.
Sarah laughed at God’s promise, and God turned her laugh of doubt into a laugh of joy.
She is called the mother of nations, and Hebrews honors her faith: “she considered Him faithful who had made the promise.”
Who Jacob was.
Jacob was the son of Isaac and Rebekah and the grandson of Abraham.
He was a twin, born just after his brother Esau, clutching his heel.
He grew up quiet and clever, his mother’s favorite, and he spent much of his early life scheming to get what he wanted.
Why God chose Jacob.
God told Rebekah before the twins were born that the older would serve the younger.
The Bible doesn’t say it was because Jacob was better — he wasn’t.
God chose to work through a flawed, scheming man, and spent decades changing him, until the trickster “Jacob” became “Israel.”
Grabbing the heel.
Even before they were born, God told Rebekah the older would serve the younger.
Esau became a hunter, Isaac’s favorite; Jacob stayed among the tents, Rebekah’s favorite.
Stew for a birthright.
The birthright meant a double inheritance and family leadership.
Esau said, “I’m about to die — what good is a birthright to me?”
He ate, drank and left, despising it.
The stolen blessing.
Isaac said, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.”
When Esau found out, he wept bitterly and vowed to kill Jacob.
Jacob fled to his uncle Laban.
A ladder to heaven.
He woke up and said, “Surely the Lord is in this place, and I was not aware of it.”
He named the place Bethel, “house of God.”
The trickster tricked.
Jacob had to work another seven years for Rachel.
He loved Rachel more, and the sisters competed through their children.
Jacob eventually had twelve sons and a daughter by four women.
Wrestling God.
The man touched Jacob’s hip and wrenched it, yet Jacob held on.
He was renamed Israel — “he struggles with God.”
He limped for the rest of his life.
He named the place Peniel: “I saw God face to face, and yet my life was spared.”
Esau runs to him.
Jacob said, “To see your face is like seeing the face of God.”
Grief and reunion.
He moved his whole family, 70 people, to Egypt during the famine.
Before dying at 147, he blessed each of his sons; their families became the twelve tribes of Israel.
Why Jacob matters today.
The whole nation of Israel is named after him, and his twelve sons became its twelve tribes.
Jacob’s life shows that God keeps His promises even through deeply imperfect people, and that wrestling honestly with God can leave you limping — and blessed.
Who Joseph was.
Joseph was the eleventh of Jacob’s twelve sons and the first son of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved most.
Born when Jacob was old, he was his father’s favorite, which made his older brothers jealous.
He was a dreamer, and God gave him the ability to understand dreams.
The favorite.
At 17 he also told on his brothers and shared dreams of their sheaves and the sun, moon and stars bowing to him.
Even his father rebuked him.
Sold.
Reuben wanted to rescue him; Judah suggested selling instead of killing.
They dipped the robe in goat’s blood.
Jacob tore his clothes and refused to be comforted.
Potiphar’s house.
She tried to seduce him day after day.
He refused: “How could I do such a wicked thing and sin against God?”
She grabbed his cloak; he ran, and she used it to frame him. He was thrown in prison.
Dreams in prison.
Even in prison, the Lord was with him and the warden put him in charge.
The cupbearer was restored, as Joseph predicted; the baker was executed.
Pharaoh’s dreams.
“I cannot do it,”
Joseph said, “but God will give Pharaoh the answer.”
He advised storing grain.
Pharaoh put him in charge of all Egypt at age 30.
The brothers bow.
He accused them of being spies, kept Simeon, and demanded they bring their youngest, Benjamin.
When he framed Benjamin with a silver cup, Judah offered himself as a slave in Benjamin’s place — showing the brothers had changed.
“I am Joseph”.
He brought his father and family to live in Egypt.
After Jacob died, the brothers feared revenge.
Joseph said: “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good, to accomplish the saving of many lives.”
He died at 110, asking that his bones be carried back to the Promised Land — which Moses did.
Why Joseph matters today.
Joseph suffered betrayal, slavery, false accusation and prison, yet stayed faithful and refused revenge.
His story is one of the clearest pictures in the Bible of God working through suffering: “You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.”
He saved Egypt and his own family from famine.
Who Moses was.
Moses was born in Egypt around the 15th or 13th century BC to Israelite slaves from the tribe of Levi, Amram and Jochebed.
His older siblings were Miriam and Aaron.
His name is related to an Egyptian word for “son” and a Hebrew word for “drawn out,” because Pharaoh’s daughter drew him out of the water.
He grew up as a member of Egypt’s royal household, then spent 40 years as a shepherd in the desert of Midian, and finally 40 years leading Israel.
Why God chose Moses.
The Bible doesn’t say God chose Moses because of his talents.
In fact, Moses argued that he wasn’t the right person and begged God to send someone else.
But Numbers calls him “more humble than anyone else on the face of the earth.”
God used his unique background — raised in Pharaoh’s palace, trained in the desert — and promised, “I will be with you.”
Saved from the Nile.
The Israelites had grown so numerous in Egypt that a new Pharaoh enslaved them and tried to control their numbers.
Moses’ sister Miriam watched the basket and arranged for their own mother to nurse him.
He grew up as a prince, educated in all the wisdom of Egypt.
Fugitive.
He thought no one saw — but the next day a Hebrew asked, “Are you thinking of killing me as you killed the Egyptian?”
In Midian he defended seven sisters at a well, married one of them, Zipporah, and worked for her father Jethro.
The burning bush.
God told him to take off his sandals because he was on holy ground.
Moses made excuse after excuse: Who am I? What’s Your name?
What if they don’t believe me? I’m not a good speaker.
Please send someone else.
God gave him signs — a staff that became a snake — and sent his brother Aaron to speak for him.
Ten plagues.
Each plague struck at Egypt’s gods — the Nile, the sun, the livestock.
Pharaoh kept promising to let them go, then hardening his heart.
Before the last plague, Israelite families sacrificed a lamb and put its blood on their doorframes so death would pass over them — the first Passover.
The Red Sea.
Moses told the terrified people, “The Lord will fight for you; you need only to be still.”
A pillar of cloud stood between them and the Egyptians all night while a strong east wind divided the water.
Afterward Moses and Miriam led the people in a song of victory.
Bread from heaven.
Manna appeared on the ground like frost — “What is it?” (man hu) gave it its name.
It tasted like wafers made with honey, and it fed Israel for 40 years.
The Ten Commandments.
“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery.
You shall have no other gods before Me.”
The commandments cover worship of God, the Sabbath, honoring parents, and not murdering, committing adultery, stealing, lying or coveting.
Moses also received instructions for the tabernacle, a portable tent where God’s presence would dwell among them.
The golden calf.
Moses even asked God to blot him out instead. God relented.
Moses asked to see God’s glory; God hid him in a cleft of the rock and passed by, proclaiming, “The Lord, the compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness.”
Moses’ face shone so brightly afterward that he wore a veil.
40 years in the wilderness.
Moses’ own patience broke once: told to speak to a rock for water, he struck it angrily instead.
Because of that, God said he would not enter the Promised Land.
How it ended.
His eyes were not weak nor his strength gone.
Deuteronomy says no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, “whom the Lord knew face to face.”
Centuries later, Moses appeared with Elijah beside Jesus at the Transfiguration — finally standing in the Promised Land.
Why Moses matters today.
Moses is the great lawgiver and prophet of the Old Testament.
Through him God freed Israel from slavery, gave the Ten Commandments, and formed a nation.
The Exodus is the defining rescue story of the Old Testament, and Jesus celebrated it at the Last Supper, giving it new meaning.
Who Aaron was.
Aaron was the older brother of Moses and Miriam, from the tribe of Levi.
While Moses grew up in the palace and fled to Midian, Aaron remained among the enslaved Israelites in Egypt.
He was a good speaker, so God chose him to be Moses’ spokesman.
The spokesman.
Aaron was three years older than Moses.
He went with Moses before Pharaoh and threw down his staff, which became a snake and swallowed the Egyptian magicians’ snakes.
Holding up his arms.
As long as Moses’ hands were raised, Israel was winning.
When his arms got tired, they sat him on a stone and held his hands up until sunset.
The golden calf.
“They gave me the gold, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf!”
It’s one of the weakest excuses in the Bible.
High priest.
“The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make His face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn His face toward you and give you peace.”
When others challenged his priesthood, his staff sprouted, blossomed and produced almonds overnight.
He died at 123 on Mount Hor.
Why Aaron matters today.
Aaron became Israel’s first high priest, and all later priests descended from him.
His failures (the golden calf) and his calling both point forward to Jesus, whom Hebrews calls the perfect High Priest.
Who Miriam was.
Miriam was the older sister of Aaron and Moses.
She is the first woman in the Bible called a prophet.
The prophet Micah later names her alongside Moses and Aaron as one of the three leaders God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt.
Watching from the reeds.
Her quick thinking meant Moses was raised by his mother in his earliest years, learning who he really was.
The song at the sea.
The Bible calls her a prophet — one of the first women given that title.
Jealousy.
The people waited for her before moving on.
She died in Kadesh before Israel entered the land.
Why Miriam matters today.
Miriam’s quick thinking saved her baby brother, and her song after the Red Sea is one of the oldest poems in the Bible.
Her story also shows God’s discipline and mercy when she grew jealous.
Who Joshua was.
Joshua, son of Nun, was from the tribe of Ephraim.
Born a slave in Egypt, he became Moses’ assistant and military commander during the wilderness years.
His original name was Hoshea, “salvation”; Moses changed it to Yehoshua, “the Lord saves” — the same name as Jesus (Yeshua).
Moses’ assistant.
He was Moses’ aide from his youth and would stay at the tent of meeting after Moses left.
His name, Yehoshua, means “the Lord saves” — the same name as Jesus.
The faithful spy.
The people wanted to stone them.
Because of their faith, they were the only adults of that generation allowed to enter the land.
Be strong and courageous.
He was told to meditate on God’s law day and night.
Crossing the Jordan.
They set up twelve stones from the riverbed as a memorial so their children would ask, “What do these stones mean?”
Jericho.
Before the battle, Joshua met a man with a drawn sword: the commander of the Lord’s army, who told him to take off his sandals, just like Moses at the burning bush.
The sun stood still.
“There has never been a day like it before or since, a day when the Lord listened to a human being.”
“As for me and my house”.
The people promised to serve the Lord, and they did as long as Joshua and the elders who outlived him were alive.
Why Joshua matters today.
Joshua led Israel into the land God had promised Abraham.
His courage came from God’s repeated promise, “I will be with you,” and his famous choice still challenges people: “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord.”
Who Caleb was.
Caleb, son of Jephunneh, was a leader from the tribe of Judah and one of the twelve spies Moses sent into Canaan. He was 40 at the time.
A different spirit.
God said Caleb had “a different spirit” and followed Him wholeheartedly.
“Give me this mountain”.
“I am still as strong today as the day Moses sent me out.”
He received Hebron as his inheritance.
Why Caleb matters today.
Caleb trusted God when the majority didn’t, waited 45 years for God’s promise, and at 85 still asked for the hardest mountain.
He shows that faith doesn’t retire.
Who Rahab was.
Rahab was a Canaanite woman living in Jericho, working as a prostitute, in a house built into the city wall.
She was an outsider in every way — not an Israelite, and with a shameful profession — yet she believed that Israel’s God was the true God.
Hiding the spies.
Her house was built into the city wall.
She told the spies, “I know that the Lord has given you this land… for the Lord your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below.”
She’d heard about the Red Sea 40 years earlier.
The scarlet cord.
When the walls fell, Joshua sent the two spies to bring out Rahab and her whole family.
Ancestor of kings.
Matthew’s genealogy includes her by name.
Hebrews and James both praise her faith.
Why Rahab matters today.
Rahab is named in Jesus’ family tree and praised for her faith in Hebrews and James.
Her story shows that God welcomes anyone who turns to Him, no matter where they come from.
Who Deborah was.
Deborah lived in the hill country of Ephraim during the time of the judges, about 1200 BC, when Israel had no king and kept falling into cycles of disobedience and oppression.
She was a prophet and Israel’s judge — its leader and settler of disputes — the only woman to hold that role.
She was married to a man named Lappidoth.
Judge under the palm.
For 20 years the Canaanite king Jabin and his general Sisera, with 900 iron chariots, had cruelly oppressed Israel.
The people cried out to God.
“Has not the Lord commanded you?”.
She told him the honor of defeating Sisera would go to a woman instead.
Victory.
Deborah’s song in Judges 5 says the stars fought from heaven and the river Kishon swept the enemy away — likely a storm that bogged down the chariots.
The land had peace for 40 years.
Why Deborah matters today.
Deborah was a woman of wisdom and courage at a time when Israel’s men hesitated.
She shows that God raises up the leaders He chooses.
Who Gideon was.
Gideon was the youngest son in a family from the clan of Abiezer, the weakest clan in the tribe of Manasseh.
For seven years the Midianites had raided Israel at harvest time, stealing crops and livestock, and the people hid in caves.
Gideon was threshing wheat secretly in a winepress when God called him.
Why God chose Gideon.
Gideon himself asked that question.
God called him “mighty warrior” while he was hiding — naming what God would make of him.
God then deliberately shrank his army so that no one could say Israel won by its own strength.
“Mighty warrior”.
Gideon answered, “If the Lord is with us, why has all this happened?”
He said his clan was the weakest and he was the least in his family.
Tearing down Baal.
The town wanted to kill him.
His father said, “If Baal really is a god, he can defend himself.”
The fleece.
God was patient with his fear.
“In order that Israel may not boast against Me that her own strength has saved her.”
Jars and torches.
The Midianites panicked and turned their swords on each other.
Later Gideon refused to be king — but made a gold ephod that became an idol for Israel.
Why Gideon matters today.
Gideon shows that God is patient with our fears and that victory comes from God, not numbers.
His later mistakes also warn that early faith must be guarded.
Who Samson was.
Samson was born to a couple from the tribe of Dan who had been unable to have children.
An angel announced his birth and said he would be a Nazirite — set apart to God — from birth.
He judged Israel for 20 years during the period when the Philistines dominated them.
Set apart.
Nazirites didn’t cut their hair, drink wine or touch dead bodies.
Samson broke every part of the vow except his hair.
The lion and the riddle.
His Philistine wedding guests pressured his bride to get the answer, and he killed thirty Philistines to pay the bet.
A cycle of revenge began.
Super strength.
He judged Israel for 20 years.
Delilah.
She lulled him to sleep on her lap and had his seven braids shaved.
“The Philistines are upon you, Samson!”
He didn’t know the Lord had left him.
They gouged out his eyes and put him to work grinding grain in prison.
The last prayer.
His hair had begun to grow back.
He prayed, “Sovereign Lord, remember me.”
Hebrews lists him among the heroes of faith.
Why Samson matters today.
Samson was given enormous strength but struggled with self-control and wasted much of his calling.
Yet in his final prayer, he turned back to God.
Hebrews lists him among the heroes of faith — a reminder of God’s grace toward deeply flawed people.
Who Ruth was.
Ruth was a Moabite woman.
Moab was a neighboring nation often hostile to Israel, and Moabites worshiped a god named Chemosh.
She married an Israelite named Mahlon whose family had moved to Moab during a famine.
After her husband died, she chose to follow her mother-in-law Naomi to Bethlehem and to worship the God of Israel.
Widowed in Moab.
Naomi was left with two daughters-in-law, Orpah and Ruth, and no way to support them.
“Your God, my God”.
Back in Bethlehem, Naomi told the women, “Don’t call me Naomi (pleasant). Call me Mara (bitter).”
Gleaning in Boaz’s field.
God’s law told farmers to leave the edges of fields for the poor and foreigners.
Boaz told his men to drop extra stalks on purpose.
At the threshing floor.
A “kinsman-redeemer” could buy back family land and marry a widow to carry on the family name.
Boaz was moved and praised her loyalty.
A grandson for Naomi.
The women of Bethlehem told Naomi that Ruth was better to her than seven sons.
Ruth is one of four women named in Jesus’ family tree in Matthew.
Why Ruth matters today.
Ruth’s loyalty and kindness turned a story of tragedy into hope.
A foreigner became the great-grandmother of King David and an ancestor of Jesus.
Her story shows God’s care for outsiders, widows and the poor.
Who Hannah was.
Hannah was one of two wives of Elkanah, from the hill country of Ephraim.
His other wife, Peninnah, had children and mocked Hannah for having none.
Every year the family traveled to Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, to worship.
Year after year.
Her husband Elkanah loved her: “Don’t I mean more to you than ten sons?”
The silent prayer.
She vowed that if God gave her a son, she would give him to the Lord for his whole life. Eli blessed her.
Keeping her promise.
Every year she made him a little robe and brought it.
God gave her three more sons and two daughters.
Her song in 1 Samuel 2 echoes in Mary’s Magnificat.
Why Hannah matters today.
Hannah poured out her pain honestly to God, kept her promise when He answered, and her son Samuel became one of Israel’s greatest leaders.
Her song of praise echoes in Mary’s song centuries later.
Who Samuel was.
Samuel was the son of Hannah and Elkanah, given to God’s service as a young child and raised at the tabernacle in Shiloh by the high priest Eli.
He became Israel’s last judge, a prophet, and the one who anointed Israel’s first two kings.
“Speak, Lord”.
God’s message was hard: judgment on Eli’s corrupt sons.
Samuel told Eli the whole truth.
Prophet and judge.
He traveled a circuit judging Israel and led them to turn from idols.
“Give us a king”.
God said, “It is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king.”
The heart, not the height.
Samuel thought the tall oldest son must be the one.
God said, “People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.”
Why Samuel matters today.
Samuel’s first prayer — “Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening” — is still a model of how to approach God.
He led Israel faithfully through its move from judges to kings.
Who Saul was.
Saul, son of Kish, was from the small tribe of Benjamin.
He was tall, handsome and humble at first.
He became Israel’s first king around 1050 BC, chosen when the people demanded a king like the other nations.
Looking for donkeys.
He was a head taller than anyone else.
At his public choosing, he hid among the baggage.
A strong start.
He won many battles against Israel’s enemies.
Doing it his way.
God rejected him as king.
An evil spirit tormented him, and young David was brought in to play the harp to calm him.
Jealous rage.
He threw spears at David and chased him through the wilderness for years.
How it ended.
Three of his sons, including Jonathan, died the same day on Mount Gilboa.
David wrote a lament: “How the mighty have fallen!”
Why Saul matters today.
Saul started with every advantage but kept choosing his own way over God’s, then let jealousy consume him.
His life is a warning: “To obey is better than sacrifice.”
Who David was.
David was the youngest of eight sons of Jesse, a farmer in Bethlehem, from the tribe of Judah.
He was the great-grandson of Ruth and Boaz.
He grew up as a shepherd, defending his flock from lions and bears, and was a gifted musician and poet.
He became Israel’s second and greatest king, reigning about 40 years around 1000 BC.
Why God chose David.
When Samuel came to anoint a king, God passed over all of David’s older, more impressive brothers and said, “The Lord does not look at the things people look at.
People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.”
Later God called David “a man after My own heart.”
The forgotten son.
God passed over all seven older sons.
When David came in, God said, “Rise and anoint him; this is the one.”
The Spirit of the Lord came on him powerfully from that day.
The giant.
He’d killed lions and bears defending his sheep. He refused Saul’s armor.
The stone struck Goliath’s forehead, and David cut off the giant’s head with the giant’s own sword.
Best friends.
Jonathan gave David his robe, sword and bow — symbolically handing over his right to the throne.
They made a covenant of friendship.
On the run.
Hundreds of outcasts gathered around him and became his mighty men.
Many psalms come from this time: “The Lord is my rock, my fortress and my deliverer.”
King in Jerusalem.
God promised David that his throne would be established forever — the promise fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David.
Bathsheba.
The prophet Nathan told David a story about a rich man stealing a poor man’s only lamb.
David was outraged — and Nathan said, “You are the man!” David confessed.
Psalm 51 is his prayer: “Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Family pain.
David wept, “O my son Absalom!
If only I had died instead of you!”
His legacy.
He passed the throne to Solomon and gathered materials for the Temple.
Jesus was born in Bethlehem, the city of David, and called “Son of David.”
Why David matters today.
David was a giant-killer, a poet, a warrior and a king — and also an adulterer and murderer who repented deeply.
God promised that his throne would last forever, a promise fulfilled in Jesus, called the “Son of David.”
His psalms still give words to people’s prayers.
Who Solomon was.
Solomon was the son of King David and Bathsheba.
He became Israel’s third king around 970 BC and reigned 40 years, a time of peace and great wealth.
God gave him extraordinary wisdom.
Ask for anything.
God was pleased and gave him wisdom — plus riches and honor he didn’t ask for.
The two mothers.
All Israel was in awe, seeing he had wisdom from God.
The Temple.
At the dedication he prayed, “The heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain You.
How much less this temple I have built!”
The Queen of Sheba.
He wrote 3,000 proverbs and 1,005 songs.
Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs are linked with him.
How it ended.
God said the kingdom would be torn from his family — though not in his lifetime.
After he died, the ten northern tribes split away.
Why Solomon matters today.
Solomon built the Temple and wrote much of Israel’s wisdom literature, including Proverbs.
But his heart drifted from God in his later years — a warning that wisdom isn’t enough without faithfulness.
Who Esther was.
Esther lived in Susa, the Persian capital, around 480 BC, in the reign of King Xerxes (Ahasuerus).
She was a Jewish orphan descended from exiles taken from Jerusalem, raised by her older cousin Mordecai.
Her Hebrew name was Hadassah, meaning “myrtle.”
An orphan in Persia.
Her people had been exiled there generations earlier.
Chosen queen.
Mordecai also uncovered a plot to assassinate the king, which was recorded but forgotten.
Haman’s plot.
He cast lots (pur) to choose the date.
“For such a time as this”.
Mordecai said, “Who knows but that you have come to your royal position for such a time as this?”
The banquets.
The night between, the king couldn’t sleep, read the records, and honored Mordecai — led through the city by Haman himself.
The Jews were allowed to defend themselves, and the feast of Purim still celebrates it.
Why Esther matters today.
The book of Esther never mentions God’s name, yet God is clearly at work behind the scenes.
Esther risked her life to save her people, and Jews still celebrate it every year at Purim.
Who Hezekiah was.
Hezekiah became king of Judah around 715 BC at age 25, following his idolatrous father Ahaz.
He reigned 29 years in Jerusalem, during the time of the prophet Isaiah and the rising Assyrian empire.
Cleaning house.
He even smashed Moses’ bronze snake, which people had started worshiping.
“There was no one like him among all the kings of Judah.”
Under siege.
He also dug a tunnel to bring water into the city — Hezekiah’s Tunnel still exists today.
One night.
Assyrian records boast of trapping Hezekiah “like a bird in a cage” — but never claim to capture Jerusalem.
15 more years.
Afterward he foolishly showed Babylonian envoys all his treasures, and Isaiah warned that Babylon would one day carry it all away.
Why Hezekiah matters today.
Hezekiah turned his nation back to God and, when facing an impossible threat, took it straight to God in prayer. God answered.
Who Josiah was.
Josiah became king of Judah around 640 BC at just eight years old.
His grandfather Manasseh and father Amon had filled the land with idol worship.
King at eight.
His grandfather Manasseh was the most wicked king in Judah’s history.
The lost book.
He realized how far the nation had strayed.
The prophetess Huldah confirmed judgment would come, but not in his lifetime because his heart was humble.
Revival.
He died at 39 in battle against Pharaoh Neco.
Jeremiah wrote laments for him.
Why Josiah matters today.
Josiah’s reforms began when he heard God’s Word read and took it seriously.
One person who responds to Scripture can change a nation.
Who Elijah was.
Elijah was a prophet from Tishbe in Gilead, east of the Jordan River, active around 860 BC in the northern kingdom of Israel.
He wore a garment of hair with a leather belt.
His name means “My God is the Lord” — exactly the message of his life, in a time when King Ahab and Queen Jezebel promoted the worship of Baal.
No rain.
Ahab and Queen Jezebel had made Baal — the supposed storm god — Israel’s official religion.
A drought was a direct challenge to Baal.
It lasted three and a half years.
The widow’s flour.
She had only enough for one last meal.
Elijah asked her to make him a small loaf first.
She did, and the jar never ran empty until the rain came.
Fire on Mount Carmel.
He mocked them: “Shout louder!
Maybe he’s sleeping or traveling.”
They cut themselves and raved all day.
Elijah had twelve jars of water poured on his sacrifice.
His prayer was simple: “Let it be known today that You are God in Israel.”
Fire consumed everything, even the water.
The people shouted, “The Lord — He is God!”
Then Elijah prayed seven times, and a small cloud became a downpour.
Burned out.
He traveled 40 days to Mount Horeb.
There came a wind, an earthquake and a fire — but God wasn’t in them.
Then a gentle whisper: “What are you doing here, Elijah?”
God told him he wasn’t alone — 7,000 had not bowed to Baal — and gave him a successor, Elisha.
Naboth’s vineyard.
Ahab said, “So you have found me, my enemy!”
Elijah foretold dogs licking Ahab’s blood and eating Jezebel — both later happened.
Chariot of fire.
The prophet Malachi promised Elijah would come again before the day of the Lord.
Jesus said John the Baptist came in Elijah’s spirit, and Elijah himself appeared at the Transfiguration.
Why Elijah matters today.
Elijah is one of the greatest prophets in the Bible.
He confronted kings, saw fire fall from heaven — and also felt burned out and alone, until God met him in a gentle whisper.
