James says he was “a human being, even as we are,” and his prayers were powerful.
Who Elisha was.
Elisha, son of Shaphat, was a farmer from Abel Meholah plowing with twelve pairs of oxen when Elijah called him.
He served as Elijah’s apprentice, then as a prophet in Israel for about 50 years.
Burning the plow.
There was no going back.
A double portion.
The Bible records about twice as many miracles for Elisha as for Elijah.
Oil and a boy raised.
The Shunammite woman had built a little room for Elisha.
He promised her a son; years later the boy died and Elisha brought him back.
Naaman’s healing.
A captive Israelite servant girl told Naaman’s wife about the prophet.
Naaman declared, “Now I know there is no God in all the world except in Israel.”
Horses and chariots of fire.
“Don’t be afraid.
Those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”
Why Elisha matters today.
Elisha’s ministry was full of compassion — for widows, families, foreigners and even enemies.
He showed that God’s power is often seen in caring for ordinary people’s needs.
Who Isaiah was.
Isaiah, son of Amoz, was a prophet in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC, during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah.
He was married and had two sons whose names carried prophetic messages.
He seems to have had access to the royal court.
Holy, holy, holy.
A seraph touched his lips with a coal from the altar: “Your guilt is taken away.”
Send me.
God warned him people wouldn’t listen.
He counseled kings Ahaz and Hezekiah.
A child is born.
Matthew quotes Isaiah 7 about Jesus’ birth.
The suffering servant.
“We all, like sheep, have gone astray… and the Lord has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.”
A scroll of Isaiah found among the Dead Sea Scrolls dates to about 100 years before Jesus.
Why Isaiah matters today.
The book of Isaiah is the Old Testament book most quoted in the New Testament.
It describes the coming Messiah in remarkable detail, and Jesus read from Isaiah to announce His own mission.
Who Jeremiah was.
Jeremiah was the son of a priest named Hilkiah from Anathoth, a village near Jerusalem.
He was called as a young man around 627 BC and prophesied for about 40 years, through the last kings of Judah and the destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon in 586 BC.
“Before you were born”.
God touched his mouth: “I have put My words in your mouth.”
An unpopular message.
God told him not to marry, as a sign of the coming disaster.
King Jehoiakim cut up his scroll and burned it piece by piece; Jeremiah dictated it again.
In the mud.
He sank into the mud with no water.
A future and a hope.
He also promised a new covenant written on hearts.
Lamentations, traditionally linked with him, mourns the fallen city and says, “His mercies are new every morning.”
Why Jeremiah matters today.
Jeremiah delivered a hard message faithfully and suffered for it.
Yet he also gave some of the most hopeful promises in the Bible, including the “new covenant”
Jesus spoke of at the Last Supper.
Who Daniel was.
Daniel was a young man from a noble family in Judah, taken to Babylon in 605 BC when King Nebuchadnezzar first conquered Jerusalem.
The Babylonians gave him a new name, Belteshazzar, and trained him for government service.
He served in the courts of Babylon and Persia for about 70 years.
Taken to Babylon.
Daniel refused the king’s rich food and asked for vegetables and water for ten days.
He and his friends ended up healthier than everyone else, and wiser.
The king’s dream.
The dream was a statue of gold, silver, bronze and iron, smashed by a rock that became a mountain — kingdoms rising and falling, and God’s kingdom lasting forever.
Writing on the wall.
Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC.
The lions’ den.
Daniel was in his 80s.
King Darius couldn’t sleep, ran to the den at dawn, and found him unharmed: “My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.”
Visions of the future.
Jesus’ favorite title for Himself, “Son of Man,” comes from this vision in Daniel 7.
Why Daniel matters today.
Daniel stayed faithful to God for a lifetime in a culture that wasn’t his own, serving his rulers well without compromising his worship.
His visions also point to God’s eternal kingdom and the “Son of Man.”
Who they were.
Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were Daniel’s friends, young men from Judah taken to Babylon and given the names Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.
They were trained with Daniel and promoted to govern the province of Babylon.
Daniel’s friends.
They trained alongside Daniel and became officials in Babylon.
“Even if He does not”.
The furnace was heated seven times hotter; the soldiers who threw them in died from the heat.
The fourth man.
They came out without even the smell of smoke.
The king praised their God and promoted them.
Why they matter today.
Their words — “even if He does not” — are one of the Bible’s greatest statements of faith: trusting God whether or not He rescues you.
Who Jonah was.
Jonah, son of Amittai, was a prophet from Gath Hepher in Galilee around 780 BC.
He had earlier prophesied that King Jeroboam II would restore Israel’s borders.
Nineveh, where God sent him, was the capital of Assyria, the most feared and brutal empire of the time.
Running away.
Assyria was Israel’s cruelest enemy.
Jonah didn’t want them to have a chance to repent.
Overboard.
The pagan sailors prayed to the Lord and offered sacrifices.
The great fish.
Jesus pointed to this as a sign: “As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of a huge fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.”
Nineveh repents.
The king wore sackcloth and sat in the dust, and ordered even the animals to fast.
Angry at mercy.
Jonah had said, “I knew You are a gracious and compassionate God… That’s why I ran.”
The book ends with God’s question unanswered.
Why Jonah matters today.
Jonah’s story is about God’s mercy reaching even Israel’s enemies — and about a prophet who didn’t want them to have it.
Jesus pointed to Jonah’s three days in the fish as a sign of His own resurrection.
Who Job was.
Job lived in the land of Uz, probably east of Israel, likely in the time of the patriarchs.
He was the greatest man among the people of the East, with large herds, many servants, seven sons and three daughters.
The Bible calls him blameless and upright.
Blameless.
God allowed Satan to test Job, but not take his life.
Everything gone.
Then he was struck with painful sores from head to foot.
His wife said, “Curse God and die!”
He replied, “Shall we accept good from God, and not trouble?”
Bad comfort.
Job poured out his anguish honestly, yet also said, “I know that my redeemer lives.”
God answers.
Job was humbled: “I spoke of things I did not understand.”
God rebuked the friends, restored Job’s fortune double, and gave him ten more children.
Why Job matters today.
Job’s story wrestles honestly with why good people suffer.
It doesn’t give a simple answer, but shows that God is present, sovereign and wise, and that bringing our honest questions to Him is not wrong.
“Who is the Lord?”.
The Bible never names him.
A hardened heart.
Some plagues his magicians copied; by the gnats they admitted, “This is the finger of God.”
The final plague.
After his own firstborn son died, Pharaoh finally told Israel to go.
How it ended.
He changed his mind once more, chased Israel with 600 chariots, and his army drowned in the Red Sea.
The champion.
Ancient manuscripts differ — some say about 6’9” — still a giant in that era.
40 days of taunting.
Morning and evening for 40 days he challenged Israel to send one man to fight him. No one dared.
How it ended.
A shepherd boy named David killed him with one stone from a sling.
A foreign queen.
She supported 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah at her table.
Naboth’s vineyard.
When Naboth wouldn’t sell his vineyard, Jezebel arranged false witnesses and had him stoned.
How it ended.
Dogs ate her body, just as Elijah had foretold.
Wounded pride.
Haman was second only to the king.
When Mordecai refused to bow, Haman plotted to kill every Jew in the empire.
Humiliated.
The king asked Haman how to honor a hero.
Thinking it was himself, he suggested a parade — then had to lead it for Mordecai.
How it ended.
Queen Esther exposed him.
He was hanged on the 75-foot gallows he built for Mordecai.
Builder and tyrant.
The historian Josephus describes his cruelty.
The Western Wall in Jerusalem is part of his Temple platform.
The wise men.
When Magi asked about a newborn King of the Jews, Herod pretended he wanted to worship Him.
How it ended.
Herod ordered all boys two and under in Bethlehem killed.
Jesus’ family escaped to Egypt. Herod died soon after.
Roman governor.
Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh and provocative toward the Jews.
“What is truth?”.
Pilate questioned Jesus: “Are You the king of the Jews?”
Jesus said His kingdom is not of this world.
Pilate asked, “What is truth?”
Washing his hands.
He released Barabbas, a murderer, instead.
He had the sign “King of the Jews” placed on the cross and refused to change it.
